title: How species change: natural selection, adaptation and new species

summary.text: A cactus has spines and a waxy skin. A lotus has stalks full of air. Each fits their place so well that it looks planned. Yet no cactus ever changed their own body to suit the desert. In every generation, living beings are born a little different, and more are born than can survive. Those whose features suit the place leave more young. Your child hunts beans on two cloths for three generations and tests two beaks in a drought year. They learn how one species can become two. They also meet Lynn Margulis, who showed that living beings joining together shaped life too.
summary.art: A cactus in sand and a lotus in a pond side by side, with a small row of beans, some dark and some pale, on a dark cloth below them.

intro.hook: A camel is born with wide feet that do not sink in sand. A lotus is born with air tubes in their stalks. Nobody fitted these parts. So how did each living being come to suit their place so well?
intro.text: For a long time, many people thought each animal changed their own body by trying hard. They thought the change was then passed on. In this unit you test a different answer with your own hands. You count the seeds in one bhindi to see how many young one plant could have. You hunt beans on a dark cloth and a pale cloth for three generations, and count who is left. You pick up seeds with tweezers and with roti tongs, in a wet year and in a drought. Then you find out how one bird became two species in the hills of South India. You also learn why your own cells hold partners that were once free bacteria.
intro.art: A child kneeling beside a dark towel scattered with pale and dark beans, dropping one bean into a steel bowl.

outcomes: By the end I can explain natural selection in four steps, using my results from the Bean Generations Test.
By the end I can describe adaptations to hot dry, wet and cold places, and the problem each solves.
By the end I can describe adaptations of predators and prey, and explain how each changes the other.
By the end I can explain why a population changes though no member changes, and why mutations come first.
By the end I can explain how one species becomes two when groups are kept apart for long.
By the end I can give Lynn Margulis's evidence that mitochondria were once free bacteria, and name three partnerships.
By the end I can give examples of evolution measured in our time, and say why slow breeders adapt slowly.

terms.meaning: Variation means the differences between living beings of the same kind. No two are exactly alike.
terms.example: Look at ten kabuli chana. They differ in size, shape and wrinkles, though all came from chana plants.
terms.art: Ten chickpeas in a row, each a slightly different size and shape.

terms.meaning: To inherit a feature is to get it from your parents through their genes. Genes are instructions stored in DNA inside every cell.
terms.example: A calf inherits the shape of her horns from her parents. She does not inherit a scar her mother got from a fence.
terms.art: A cow and her calf with the same curved horns.

terms.meaning: A generation is all the young born at about the same time. Parents are one generation and their children are the next.
terms.example: You, your mother and your grandmother are three generations. Mosquitoes can pass through a generation in two or three weeks.
terms.art: A grandmother, a mother and a girl standing in a row.

terms.meaning: A population is all the living beings of one kind who live in one place. They can breed with each other.
terms.example: All the house crows in Chennai form one population. All the chital deer in Bandipur form another.
terms.art: A flock of house crows on the wires and rooftops of one city street.

terms.meaning: Natural selection is the way a population changes over generations. Members whose features suit the place leave more young, so those features become more common.
terms.example: In a drought on a small island, finches with deeper beaks survived more often. The next generation had deeper beaks on average.
terms.art: Two finches side by side, one with a deeper beak cracking a hard spiky seed.

terms.meaning: An adaptation is an inherited feature that helps a living being survive and have young in their place.
terms.example: A camel's wide feet are an adaptation to soft sand. A lotus's air-filled stalks are an adaptation to airless mud.
terms.art: A camel's wide foot on sand beside a cut lotus stalk showing air channels.

terms.meaning: The environment is everything around a living being. It includes the weather, the water, the food and all the other living beings there.
terms.example: The environment of a Thar desert lizard is hot sand, little water, insects to eat and hawks overhead.
terms.art: A lizard on hot sand with a hawk circling above and a beetle nearby.

terms.meaning: A predator is an animal who hunts and eats other animals.
terms.example: A tiger is a predator of chital deer. A house lizard is a predator of moths.
terms.art: A house lizard on a wall creeping towards a moth near a tube light.

terms.meaning: Prey are the animals a predator hunts. One animal can be a predator and also be prey.
terms.example: A frog is prey for a snake, and the same frog is a predator of flies.
terms.art: A frog catching a fly while a snake watches the frog from the grass.

terms.meaning: Camouflage is a colour, pattern or shape that makes a living being hard to see against their background.
terms.example: The orange oakleaf butterfly of Indian forests closes their wings and looks like a dry leaf.
terms.art: A butterfly with closed wings that look exactly like a brown dry leaf on a twig.

terms.meaning: Mimicry is when one species looks like another species that predators avoid.
terms.example: The female common mormon butterfly is harmless. Many look like the common rose butterfly, who tastes bad to birds.
terms.art: Two butterflies with very similar black, white and red wings, one labelled 'tastes bad' and one labelled 'harmless'.

terms.meaning: A mutation is a change in DNA, made by chance when a cell copies DNA. Mutations are where new variations come from.
terms.example: One chance mutation long ago let some adult humans keep digesting milk. Their children inherited it.
terms.art: A long ribbon of letters being copied, with one letter in the copy drawn in a different colour.

terms.meaning: A species is a group of living beings who can breed together and have young who can also have young. Scientists do not all agree on this meaning.
terms.example: Horses and donkeys are two species. Their young, the mule, cannot have young of her own.
terms.art: A horse, a donkey and a mule standing together.

terms.meaning: Selective breeding is when people choose which plants or animals become parents, to get features that people want.
terms.example: Farmers bred cabbage, cauliflower and knol khol from one wild plant, by saving seed from the plants they liked.
terms.art: A cabbage, a cauliflower and a knol khol on a kitchen counter.

terms.meaning: Symbiosis means two different species living closely together. In many cases both partners gain.
terms.example: A lichen on a tree trunk is a fungus and an alga living as one. The alga makes sugar and the fungus holds water.
terms.art: A grey-green lichen patch on bark, with a zoom circle showing fungus threads wrapped around round green cells.

terms.meaning: Mitochondria are tiny parts inside your cells that release energy from food using oxygen. Their ancestors were free bacteria.
terms.example: A muscle cell in your leg holds thousands of mitochondria. Each has their own small loop of DNA.
terms.art: A cell drawn large with many small bean-shaped mitochondria inside, one zoomed to show a loop of DNA.

terms.meaning: Coevolution is when two species change over generations in answer to each other.
terms.example: As deer became faster, the tigers who hunted them became better at stalking. Each selected the other.
terms.art: A tiger crouched in grass watching a chital whose head is raised and ears are turned towards the tiger.

terms.meaning: A species is extinct when their last member has died. More than 99 in every 100 species that ever lived are extinct.
terms.example: The cheetah became extinct in India in the 1950s. Cheetahs from Africa were brought to Kuno in 2022.
terms.art: An old photograph-style drawing of a cheetah on Indian grassland.

explanations.definition: Natural selection is the way a population changes over generations. Members whose features suit the place leave more young, so those features become more common.
explanations.description: Natural selection needs four things. First, the members of a population vary. Second, many of their variations are inherited. Third, more young are born than can survive. Fourth, members whose features suit the place survive more often and leave more young. When this repeats for many generations, the whole population changes. No single member has to change. The place does the selecting, through its weather, food, predators and diseases. Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace both worked this out, and published it together in 1858.
examples: In the Bean Generations Test, you start with 15 dark and 15 pale beans on a dark cloth. The hunter catches more pale beans, so each new generation has more dark beans.
In 1977, a drought on the island of Daphne Major left only large, hard seeds. Finches with deeper beaks survived more often, and their chicks inherited deeper beaks.
DDT is a poison that was sprayed on mosquitoes across India from the 1950s. A few mosquitoes survived it and had young. In many places DDT stopped working within some years.

In Gorongosa in Mozambique, ivory hunters killed elephants with tusks during a war from 1977 to 1992. Before the war about 2 in 10 females had no tusks. Among females born after it, about 3 in 10 had none.
explanations.art: Four small panels in a row: beetles of different shades, a beetle with her young of the same shade, a bird eating some beetles, and a later group that is mostly one shade.

explanations.concept: Adaptations: features that fit a place
explanations.definition: An adaptation is an inherited feature that helps a living being survive and have young in their environment.
explanations.description: Every place sets problems. A hot, dry place has little water and strong sun. A wet place has water all around but little air in the mud. A cold place has snow, frozen ground and little food in winter. An adaptation is a feature that solves one of these problems. A way of behaving can be an adaptation too, such as sleeping through the winter or feeding only at night. A living being is born with their adaptations. Natural selection built each one over many generations, because members with a slightly better version left more young. Most adaptations also have a cost. Thick fur keeps a yak warm in Ladakh, and would overheat the same yak in Chennai.
examples: Hot and dry: a cactus has spines in place of flat leaves, a waxy skin and a thick stem that stores water. A camel has wide feet for sand and a hump of fat as a food store. Long eyelashes keep out blowing sand. The khejri tree of the Thar has roots that go many metres down to water.

Wet: a lotus has flat floating leaves that reach the light. Their stalks are full of air channels that carry air down to the roots. A fish has gills that take in oxygen dissolved in water. A duck has webbed feet. Mangrove trees in the Sundarbans push breathing roots up out of the mud. Seabirds such as gulls have waterproof feathers, and glands near the eyes that remove salt.

Cold: a deodar or a fir has a cone shape and sloping branches, so heavy snow slides off. Their needles have a waxy coat and lose little water, and thick bark protects the trunk. A snow leopard has thick fur and wide, furry paws. A Himalayan marmot hibernates, which means sleeping deeply through the winter.
Behaviour: bar-headed geese migrate over the Himalaya to spend the winter in India. The Indian gerbil of the Thar stays in a cool burrow by day and feeds at night.
explanations.art: Three panels: a cactus and a camel in a desert, a lotus and a duck on a pond, and a deodar and a snow leopard on a snowy slope.

explanations.concept: Predators and prey change each other
explanations.definition: A predator has adaptations for catching prey, and prey have adaptations for escaping. Each one is part of the other's environment, so each selects the other.
explanations.description: Predators need to find, reach and hold their prey. Many have eyes at the front of the head, which lets them judge distance. Others have speed, a smooth narrow shape called streamlined, camouflage, venom, traps such as webs, sharp teeth and claws, or teamwork. Prey need to notice danger and get away. Many have eyes at the sides of the head, which lets them see almost all around. Others live in herds, give alarm calls, run fast, or carry shells. Some fight back with horns, stings or spines. Some hide by camouflage. Some warn predators with bright colours that they taste bad. Some harmless species copy those colours, which is called mimicry. When prey become faster over generations, only the better hunters among the predators eat well and leave young. Each change in the predators selects a change in the prey, and each change in the prey selects a change in the predators. Scientists call this coevolution.
examples: A tiger has forward-facing eyes, stripes that hide her in tall grass, and soft paws for stalking. A chital deer has eyes at the sides, lives in a herd and gives a sharp alarm call.
Dholes, the wild dogs of Indian forests, hunt in packs. A spider traps insects in a web. A cobra stops prey with venom.
An Indian star tortoise pulls into a hard shell. A porcupine raises long quills.
In 1862 Henry Walter Bates described harmless butterflies in the Amazon that look like bad-tasting ones. In India, many female common mormon butterflies look like the bad-tasting common rose.
explanations.art: A tiger half hidden in tall dry grass, and a herd of chital with one deer looking straight at the tiger, tail raised.

explanations.concept: Where new variations come from: mutation
explanations.definition: A mutation is a change in DNA, made by chance when a cell copies DNA. Mutations are the source of new variations.
explanations.description: DNA holds the instructions for building a body, written in a code of four chemical letters. Each time a cell divides, the cell copies billions of letters, and a few copying mistakes slip through. Radiation and some chemicals can also damage DNA and cause mutations. These mistakes are mutations. Most mutations change nothing that matters. Some do harm, and a few help. A mutation in an egg cell, a sperm cell or a seed can be inherited. Each human baby is born with roughly 60 new mutations that neither parent had. A mutation appears by chance. It does not appear because the living being needs it. In 1952 Esther Lederberg and Joshua Lederberg showed this with bacteria. An antibiotic is a medicine that kills bacteria. Bacteria that could survive an antibiotic were already present before the bacteria ever met the antibiotic. So the variation comes first, and selection comes afterwards. Having two parents also makes variation, because each child gets a new mix of their parents' genes.
examples: In the activity One New Bean, a single dark bean among 29 pale beans stands for a new mutation. On a dark cloth, the dark bean's descendants can spread through the group in a few generations.
A chance mutation lets some adult humans keep digesting the sugar in milk. In peoples who herded cattle, this mutation spread over the last several thousand years.
Most mutations are never noticed. You carry dozens that do nothing you can see.
explanations.art: A strip of DNA letters being copied, with one changed letter circled, and three arrows to the words 'no effect', 'harm' and 'help', the first arrow thickest.

explanations.definition: A new species can form when a population is split into groups that cannot meet. Each group changes in their own way, until the two can no longer breed together.
explanations.description: First, something splits a population. It may be a sea, a river, a mountain range or a stretch of land where that species cannot live. Next, each group meets different conditions. Different mutations appear in each group, and natural selection keeps different variations. The groups cannot mix their genes, so the differences add up. After many thousands of generations, the two groups may differ in size, colour, song and the season when they breed. If they meet again, they no longer choose each other as mates, or their young cannot have young. Now they are two species. This is how one ancestor can leave many species. The two cloths in the Bean Generations Test show the start of this: two groups that begin the same and end different.
examples: The sholakili is a small songbird of cool hilltop forests in the Western Ghats. The Palghat Gap is a hot, low gap about 30 kilometres wide, between Coimbatore and Palakkad. North of the gap lives the Nilgiri sholakili. South of the gap lives the white-bellied sholakili. They were one species millions of years ago.
About 18 species of Darwin's finches live on the Galápagos Islands and Cocos Island. All descend from one species that arrived more than a million years ago.
Blind catfish called Horaglanis live in wells and underground water in Kerala. Their ancestors were cut off from surface streams and changed in the dark.
On Daphne Major, a male finch from another island arrived in 1981. Within a few generations, his descendants were breeding only with each other.
explanations.art: A map of the southern Western Ghats with two green hill ranges and a pale low gap between them, and a small bird drawn on each side with a different belly colour.

explanations.description: Scientists use the word 'species' every day. Yet they do not agree on one meaning that works for all of life. The reason comes from how species form. One species becomes two slowly, so at any moment some groups are part of the way there. Nature has no sharp line for us to find.
examples: A horse and a donkey can have a mule, but a mule cannot have young. So horses and donkeys count as two species.
Lions and tigers have had cubs together in zoos, and some of those cubs have had young. Yet in the wild they live as two species.
Greenish warblers live in a ring of forests around the Tibetan Plateau. Neighbouring groups breed together along the ring, but where the two ends meet in Siberia, the birds do not.

perspectives.who: Ernst Mayr, a German-American biologist, in 1942
perspectives.explanation: A species is a group whose members can breed with each other in nature and have fertile young. Members of two species cannot. This works well for most animals with two parents.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study bacteria and many plants
perspectives.explanation: Bacteria copy themselves and never breed in pairs, and many plant species cross easily. So the breeding rule fails for most of life. They group living beings by how different their DNA is.
Nobody can test whether two fossil animals could breed. They must use the shape of bones and shells, and accept that the line between species is partly our choice.

explanations.art: A horse, a donkey and a mule in a row, with a question mark over a pair of small green birds singing on two different branches.

explanations.concept: Cooperation in evolution: Lynn Margulis and the cell inside a cell
explanations.definition: Symbiosis is two different species living closely together. Sometimes two partners join so fully that they become one new kind of living being.
explanations.description: Inside almost every cell of your body are mitochondria, which release energy from food using oxygen. In 1967 the American biologist Lynn Margulis argued that mitochondria were once free bacteria. More than 1.5 billion years ago, a larger cell took in a bacterium and did not digest them. The bacterium gained food and shelter. The larger cell gained a partner who could use oxygen to release far more energy. Their descendants could no longer live apart. Later, some of these cells took in a second partner, a bacterium that could photosynthesise, which means making food from sunlight. That partner became the chloroplast, the green part of a plant cell. Her paper is said to have been turned down by about fifteen journals before one printed it. The evidence is strong. Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own DNA, in a loop like the DNA of bacteria. They make more of themselves by splitting in two, as bacteria do. They are wrapped in two membranes. In the 1970s and 1980s, scientists read their DNA and found that it matches the DNA of living bacteria. So every animal, plant and fungus descends from a partnership. Natural selection still works on partners: a partnership that helps both leaves more young.
examples: A lichen is a fungus and an alga, or a fungus and a photosynthesising bacterium, living as one body.
Pulse plants such as chana and moong house bacteria in small lumps on their roots. The bacteria turn nitrogen from the air into food the plant can use.
A coral animal houses tiny algae who share the sugar they make from sunlight.
A cow cannot digest grass alone. Microbes in her stomach break the grass down, and both are fed.
Each kind of fig tree has their own kind of tiny fig wasp. The wasp carries the fig's pollen, and the fig feeds the wasp's young.
explanations.art: A large rounded cell holding a small bean-shaped bacterium wrapped in two thin skins, and an arrow from an oxygen bubble into the small partner.

explanations.concept: Do living beings help steer their own evolution?
explanations.description: Living beings choose where to live, what to eat and whom to mate with. Many also build: nests, burrows, dams and webs. These choices change which features help them, so they change the selection on their own descendants. Scientists agree that this happens. They disagree about how much it matters.
examples: Thousands of years ago, some peoples began to herd cattle and drink their milk. That choice made the milk-digesting mutation useful, and it spread in those peoples.

Earthworms change the soil they live in by pulling leaves down and mixing it. Charles Darwin wrote his last book about them, in 1881. Each new generation of earthworms inherits soil that their ancestors changed.
A beaver builds a dam and makes a pond. The beaver's young grow up in a pond, and selection works on them there.

perspectives.explanation: Mutations arise by chance, and the environment selects among them. A habit such as dam-building is itself an inherited feature that selection shaped. Nothing more is needed to explain evolution.

perspectives.who: Mary Jane West-Eberhard, an American biologist, in 2003
perspectives.explanation: Behaviour and flexible bodies often change first. An animal tries a new food or a new place. Later, selection favours genes that suit the new way of life. She wrote that genes are often followers, not leaders.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study niche construction, such as John Odling-Smee and Kevin Laland
perspectives.explanation: Living beings make part of their own environment and pass that changed environment to their young. So young inherit two things, their genes and a changed place, and both shape evolution.

explanations.art: A beaver's dam holding back a pond, with a young beaver swimming, and an earthworm pulling a leaf into soil in a corner panel.

explanations.concept: 'Fittest' does not mean strongest, and evolution has no top
explanations.definition: In biology, 'fit' means suited to the place and so leaving more surviving young there. It does not mean strong, fast, big or clever.
explanations.description: The phrase 'survival of the fittest' was first used by Herbert Spencer in 1864, and Darwin later borrowed it. Many people take it to mean that the strongest win. The evidence says otherwise. Which feature is fit depends on the place and the year. A deep beak is fit in a drought. A small beak is fit after heavy rain. Being small, slow or blind can be fit. Evolution also has no ladder with humans at the top. Every species alive today has an equally long history, going back to the same first cells. A bacterium, a moss, a crow and a human are all well adapted to the lives they lead. Humans are one animal species among millions, still evolving like the rest.
examples: In the Drought Year Test, the roti tongs collect enough food in the drought year. The tweezers collect enough in the wet year. Neither beak is the better beak everywhere.
Blind catfish in Kerala's wells have no working eyes. In total darkness, eyes cost energy and bring nothing, so fish without them left more young.
Penguins descend from birds who flew. Their wings became flippers, which are better for swimming after fish.
Bacteria have lived on Earth for more than 3.5 billion years. They live in more places than any animal.
explanations.art: A crossed-out ladder with a human at the top, and beside it a wide branching bush with a bacterium, a moss, a crow, a fish and a human each at the tip of a branch.

agreed.text: Members of every population vary, and many variations are inherited.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can measure the variation in a handful of seeds or a class of children. Plant and animal breeders have used inherited variation for thousands of years, and DNA now shows the differences directly.

agreed.text: Natural selection changes populations, and it has been measured as it happens.
agreed.evidence: Rosemary and Peter Grant measured finch beaks on Daphne Major for 40 years. They saw beaks change after droughts and rains. Bacteria become resistant to antibiotics, and mosquitoes to poisons, within years.

agreed.text: New variations begin as chance mutations. They do not appear because they are needed.
agreed.evidence: In 1952 Esther and Joshua Lederberg tested bacteria with an antibiotic. The bacteria able to survive were present before the antibiotic was added.

agreed.text: All living beings share one ancestor, and new species form when populations split.
agreed.evidence: All life uses the same DNA code. Family trees built from DNA match those built from fossils and bodies. Islands and separated hilltops hold close relatives that differ from each other.

agreed.text: Mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from bacteria that once lived free.
agreed.evidence: Both have their own loop of DNA, both multiply by splitting, and their DNA matches that of living bacteria.

agreed.text: A feature gained during one lifetime, such as strong muscles or a scar, is not passed on through the genes.
agreed.evidence: In the 1880s August Weismann cut the tails off mice for many generations. Every new litter was born with tails of normal length.

challenging.claim: Animals change their bodies by effort, and pass the change to their young.
challenging.who: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, a French naturalist, in 1809
challenging.for: It seems to fit what we see. A giraffe's long neck looks like the result of stretching for leaves over many generations.
challenging.against: A weightlifter's child is not born with big muscles. Weismann's mice were born with tails after many generations of cut tails. The genes in egg and sperm cells are not rewritten by exercise.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of how animals come to fit their places. The idea was tested and found wrong.

challenging.claim: Natural selection is always too slow for a person to see.
challenging.who: Charles Darwin and most scientists until the 1970s
challenging.for: Big changes, such as fins turning into legs, do take millions of years. Nobody has watched one of those happen.
challenging.against: The Grants measured a change in finch beaks after one drought year. Bacteria in laboratories and insects on farms change within a few years.
challenging.context: This card is about whether evolution can be watched and measured in a human lifetime.

challenging.claim: The biggest steps in evolution came from living beings joining together, not from small mutations.
challenging.who: Lynn Margulis, in books up to 2002
challenging.for: The first complex cell came from two beings joining. So did the first plant cell. Lichens and corals are also joined beings.
challenging.against: Most biologists accept those cases but say they are rare. They find that most new species arise from mutations and selection in separated groups, with no joining.
challenging.context: This card is about how much of evolution comes from cooperation and joining, and how much from small inherited changes.

challenging.claim: Most changes in DNA neither help nor harm, and they spread by chance alone.
challenging.who: Motoo Kimura, a Japanese biologist, in 1968
challenging.for: When scientists compare the DNA of related species, most differences sit where they change nothing in the body. Chance explains those well.
challenging.against: Features such as beaks, eyes and wings fit their uses too well for chance alone. Selection is still needed to explain adaptations. Scientists argue about the share of each.
challenging.context: This card is about how much of the change in DNA is caused by chance, with no selection at all.

challenging.claim: Living beings steer their own evolution through what they choose and build.
challenging.who: Mary Jane West-Eberhard, John Odling-Smee, Kevin Laland and others
challenging.for: Herding cattle made a milk-digesting mutation useful in humans. Beavers, earthworms and termites live in places their ancestors built.
challenging.against: Many biologists reply that choosing and building are inherited features too, already explained by natural selection. They see no need for a new idea.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the behaviour of living beings leads evolution or only follows it.

big_questions.q: In the Bean Generations Test, no bean changed colour, yet the group changed. So what is it that evolves: one living being, or a population?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you counted. Could you have seen any change by watching a single bean?

big_questions.q: A mutation is a copying mistake. Can a mistake be a good thing?
big_questions.hint: Think about the single dark bean in One New Bean. What would have happened on the dark cloth with no new bean at all?

big_questions.q: A sholakili chick always belongs to the same species as her parents. So when did one species become two?
big_questions.hint: Think about a child growing taller. On which day did she stop being short?

big_questions.q: The mitochondria in your cells descend from free bacteria. Are you one living being, or many living together?
big_questions.hint: Your mitochondria have their own DNA and split on their own. But neither you nor they can live apart.

big_questions.q: If the place decides which features help, can any species be called better than another?
big_questions.hint: Remember which beak did well in the drought year and which did well in the wet year.

big_questions.q: Mosquitoes kept up with our poisons within a few years. A bustard cannot keep up with power lines. Why can some species keep up with fast change and others not?
big_questions.hint: Compare how many young each has, and how long a generation takes.

story.title: What the Dry Year Left
story.note: Thenmozhi, Paati, Murugesan Mama and their fields are made up, and so are the counts. These things are real: the Kolli Hills are in Namakkal district in Tamil Nadu, and the road up has seventy hairpin bends. Farmers there grow ragi and other millets, and many keep their own mixed seed. Storing seed in a clay pot with ash and dried neem leaves is an old practice. In a mixed crop, plants that ripen early and root deeply are likeliest to give grain in a dry year.
text: Every October, Thenmozhi rode the bus up seventy hairpin bends to her grandmother's village in the Kolli Hills. Paati grew ragi on a slope behind the house. Thenmozhi thought it was the untidiest field on the whole hill.

Next door, Murugesan Mama's ragi stood like children at a school assembly. Every plant was the same height, and every head of grain turned brown in the same week. He bought his seed each year in a sealed packet from a shop in Namakkal.

Paati's field had tall plants and short ones. Some heads were already brown while others were still green. Some heads were closed like fists and some were open like fingers. Paati had never bought a seed in her life. She kept her own, as her mother had, in a clay pot with ash and dried neem leaves.
"Why don't you sow Mama's seed?" Thenmozhi asked. "His field looks so neat."
"Neat is nice," said Paati, "in a good year."
The year Thenmozhi turned ten, the rain came in June and then stopped. July was dry. August was dry. When her bus came round the last bend in October, the hill was the wrong colour.
Murugesan Mama's field was straw from end to end. Every plant was still the same height. Every plant had died in the same week. He stood at the edge with his hands behind his back and said nothing.

Paati's field looked almost as bad. Most of her plants were straw too. But here and there a plant was still standing, green at the foot, with a small head of grain. Thenmozhi walked every row and counted them. There were thirty-one, in a field that had held thousands.
She looked at them closely. Nearly all were short plants, the ones she had thought ugly. Their heads were small, and they had ripened early.
"A whole field," said Thenmozhi, "for two handfuls."
Paati did not seem upset. She cut the thirty-one heads herself, one at a time, and tied them in a separate cloth. That evening she rubbed out the grain. Thenmozhi fetched the cooking pot.
"Not that pot," said Paati. "These we do not eat."
"But we have so little!"
"These are the ones who managed," said Paati. She poured the grain into the clay seed pot and pressed the lid down.

Before she left, Thenmozhi pulled up two plants from the field. One was a tall dead plant and one was a short living plant. The tall plant's roots were a shallow mat, no longer than her hand. The short plant's roots went down longer than her arm. She turned them over and over, and did not know what to make of them.

The next June, Paati sowed the grain from the thirty-one plants at the top of the slope. She sowed her old mixed seed lower down. The rain was fair that year and the year after, and Thenmozhi forgot about the roots.

When she was twelve, the rain failed again. Her bus came round the last bend, and Murugesan Mama's new packet of seed had become straw, exactly as before. Paati's lower field was mostly straw. But at the top of the slope the ragi stood. The plants were thin and their heads were small, but they were alive. Thenmozhi began to count them and gave up after four hundred.

She sat down on the stone bund at the edge of the field. Paati had not carried more water up the slope. Nobody could, on that hill. The plants at the top had not grown deep roots because the year was dry. They were the children of the thirty-one, and the thirty-one had been deep-rooted and quick from the day they sprouted.

Then she saw the whole of it. The first dry year had gone through the mixed field and removed every plant that needed more water than there was. It had left the few who could do with less. Their grain had grown into plants like themselves. Now there were hundreds.
"Paati," she said, "you did not change the ragi. The dry year chose. You only kept what the dry year left."
Paati laughed. "My mother said the same thing in fewer words. She said the bad year is the real seed keeper."
That evening Thenmozhi noticed a second clay pot, behind the first. "What is in that one?"
"The tall ones," said Paati. "And the late ones."
"But they die in a dry year! Why keep them?"

"In a dry year, yes. Fifteen years ago it rained for forty days without a stop. The short, early ones ripened in the rain, and their grain rotted on the stalk. The tall, late ones fed this house. I do not know which year is coming, kanna. So I keep some of everyone."
Thenmozhi went out and looked at the lower field for a long time. The field was not untidy. Every kind of plant there had come through some year that had finished off the others.
In the morning she asked for a spoonful of grain from each pot, to take down the seventy bends to her balcony in Salem.
story.epiphany: For the parent: this is natural selection in a field. The ragi plants varied in height, roots and ripening time, and they passed these features to their seed. The drought removed the plants that needed more water. The survivors became the parents, so the next crop was mostly deep-rooted and early. No plant changed during the dry year. The second pot shows that no feature is best in every year. A population with more variation can come through more kinds of trouble. Murugesan Mama's plants were all alike, so one bad year took them all.
ask: Why did all of Murugesan Mama's plants die in the same week?
Thenmozhi said the dry year chose. What did she mean?
Did any ragi plant grow deeper roots because the year was dry? How do you know?
Why does Paati keep the seed of tall, late plants that die in a dry year?
Which is safer for a farmer over twenty years: a field where all plants are alike, or a mixed field? Give your reasons.
