games.title: Feature and Problem: the adaptation cards
games.context: This is a card game about adaptations. Each card names a feature of a plant or an animal. You say which problem of their place the feature solves.

printables.title: 24 adaptation cards to cut out (the problem is on the back)

items.f: Cactus: spines where other plants have flat leaves
items.b: Problem: losing water in hot, dry air. A spine has very little surface, so little water escapes. Spines also keep thirsty animals away.

items.f: Cactus: a thick green stem with a waxy skin
items.b: Problem: long months with no rain. The stem stores water and the wax slows its escape. The green stem also makes the food.

items.f: Camel: a hump of fat
items.b: Problem: weeks with little food in the desert. The hump is a food store. It holds fat, not water.

items.f: Camel: wide, flat feet
items.b: Problem: sinking into soft sand. A wide foot spreads the camel's weight over more sand.

items.f: Khejri tree of the Thar: roots that go many metres down
items.b: Problem: no water near the surface. Deep roots reach water far underground.

items.f: Lotus: big flat leaves that float
items.b: Problem: getting sunlight when you grow in a pond. Floating leaves lie on top of the water, in full light.

items.f: Lotus: stalks full of air channels
items.b: Problem: no air in pond mud. The channels carry air down to the roots.

items.f: Fish: gills
items.b: Problem: breathing under water. Gills take in the oxygen that is dissolved in water.

items.f: Duck: webbed feet
items.b: Problem: pushing against water. A webbed foot is a wide paddle.

items.f: Mangrove tree of the Sundarbans: roots that stick up out of the mud
items.b: Problem: airless, salty mud. The upright roots take in air at low tide.

items.f: Deodar: a cone shape with sloping branches
items.b: Problem: heavy snow that breaks branches. Snow slides off the slope.

items.f: Fir: thin needles with a waxy coat
items.b: Problem: frozen ground gives no water in winter. Thin, waxy needles lose very little water.

items.f: Snow leopard: thick fur and wide, furry paws
items.b: Problem: cold, and deep snow. The fur keeps heat in. Wide paws spread her weight on snow.

items.f: Yak: a long, thick coat and large lungs
items.b: Problem: cold and thin air high in Ladakh. The coat holds heat, and large lungs take in more air.

items.f: Himalayan marmot: sleeps deeply all winter
items.b: Problem: no food under the snow. Hibernating uses very little energy until spring.

items.f: Tiger: eyes at the front of the head
items.b: Problem: judging the distance to prey. Two eyes facing the same way let a predator judge distance well.

items.f: Tiger: stripes
items.b: Problem: getting close without being seen. Stripes break up the tiger's outline in tall grass and shade.

items.f: Cobra: venom
items.b: Problem: prey that fights back or runs. Venom stops prey quickly.

items.f: Spider: a sticky web
items.b: Problem: catching insects who fly. The web traps them, so the spider need not chase.

items.f: Chital deer: eyes at the sides of the head
items.b: Problem: a predator may come from any side. Side eyes see almost all the way around.

items.f: Chital deer: living in a herd, with alarm calls
items.b: Problem: one deer cannot watch everywhere. In a herd, many eyes watch and one call warns all.

items.f: Indian star tortoise: a hard shell
items.b: Problem: teeth and claws. The tortoise pulls head and legs inside the shell.

items.f: Common mormon butterfly: many females look like the bad-tasting common rose
items.b: Problem: birds who eat butterflies. Birds who have learned to avoid the common rose avoid the look-alike too. This is mimicry.

items.f: Orange oakleaf butterfly: closed wings look like a dry leaf
items.b: Problem: being seen by birds. On a twig, the butterfly is taken for a dead leaf. This is camouflage.

printables.title: Score sheet
items: One row for each player. Make a mark for every card you keep.

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, feature side up.
On your turn, read the top card aloud. Say which problem the feature solves, and what kind of place sets that problem.
Turn the card over. If you named the problem, keep the card. If not, put the card at the bottom of the pile.
For one extra mark, say what would happen to that plant or animal without the feature.
The game ends when the pile is finished. The player with the most marks wins.
Playing alone: try to keep 20 of the 24 cards on the first time through.

setup.art: A pile of cut-out cards on a table, the top one reading 'Camel: wide, flat feet', with a pencil and a score sheet.
setup.caption: 1. Put the pile feature side up.

setup.art: A child holding a card and speaking, with a thought bubble showing a foot sinking in sand.
setup.caption: 2. Read the card. Say which problem the feature solves.

setup.art: The same card turned over to show the answer, and the child making a mark on the score sheet.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over to check. Keep the card if you were right.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 24 cards. 2. Shuffle them. 3. Put them in a pile, feature side up. 4. Draw a score row for each player.
flow.say: Every card names one feature. Each feature solves a problem that a place sets, such as heat, cold, deep water or a predator.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and mix them. Put them in a pile. Draw a score row.
flow.context: This is the first step of Feature and Problem. Here you set up the adaptation cards.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to read the top card. 2. Say the problem the feature solves. 3. Turn the card over to check. 4. Ask what would happen without the feature.
flow.say: Read the card aloud. Which problem does this feature solve? What would happen to this living being without it?
flow.kid: Read the card. Say the problem the feature solves. Then turn the card over.

ask.q: A camel's hump holds fat, not water. Why is one big hump better than fat spread all over the body?
good: Fat all over would keep heat in, like a blanket.
With the fat in one place, the rest of the body can lose heat.

flow.parent: A good answer names a problem, not only a place. 'Because the camel lives in a desert' is a start. Ask what the desert does to feet.
flow.context: This is the main part of Feature and Problem. Here you read each adaptation card and say which problem the feature solves.

flow.do: 1. Count the marks. 2. Sort all 24 cards into three piles: features against weather, features for catching, features for escaping. 3. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Sort the cards into three piles: weather, catching and escaping. Which pile is biggest? Did anyone give these features to the animals and plants?
flow.kid: Count your marks. Sort the cards into three piles. Which pile is biggest?

check.q: A chital deer has eyes at the sides of the head. A tiger's eyes face forward. Why the difference?
options: Deer must see all around, tigers must judge distance
Deer eyes are weaker than tiger eyes
The tiger hunts only at night
check.why: Side eyes give a view almost all the way round, which helps prey notice danger. Forward eyes give two views of the same thing, which helps a predator judge how far to leap. If you chose 'weaker eyes', remember that both see well. They are placed for different jobs.

flow.context: This is the last step of Feature and Problem. Here you sort the adaptation cards by the kind of problem they solve.

games.title: Partner Pairs: a memory game about living together
games.context: This is a memory game about symbiosis, which means two species living closely together. You find the two partners and say what each one gives the other.

printables.title: 16 partner cards to cut out
items: Fig tree: I give a safe home and food to the young of one tiny wasp.
Fig wasp: I carry pollen from one fig to the next.
Chana plant: I give sugar and a home in small lumps on my roots.
Root bacteria: I turn nitrogen from the air into food the plant can use.
Coral animal: I give a safe home in sunlit water.
Coral algae: I make sugar from sunlight and share it.
Cow: I give a warm stomach and a steady supply of grass.
Stomach microbes: I break down tough grass that the cow cannot digest alone.
Lichen fungus: I hold water and grip the rock or bark.
Lichen alga: I make sugar from sunlight for both of us.
Sea anemone: My stinging arms keep one small fish safe.
Clownfish: I chase away the fish who nibble the anemone.
Pumpkin flower: I give nectar and pollen as food.
Bee: I carry pollen from flower to flower.
Your body cell: I give food and shelter.
Mitochondrion: I release energy from food, using oxygen.

rules: Shuffle the 16 cards and lay them face down in four rows of four.
On your turn, turn over two cards and read them aloud.
If the two are partners, say what each gives the other. Then keep the pair and take another turn.
If they are not partners, turn them face down again in the same places.
The game ends when all eight pairs are found. The player with the most pairs wins.
Playing alone: count your turns. Play again and try to finish in fewer turns.

setup.art: Sixteen small cards face down in four rows of four on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the 16 cards face down.

setup.art: A child turning over two cards that read 'Fig tree' and 'Fig wasp'.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over two cards and read them.

setup.art: The child holding the matched pair and speaking to a parent.
setup.caption: 3. If they are partners, say what each one gives. Keep the pair.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 16 cards. 2. Shuffle them. 3. Lay them face down in four rows of four.
flow.say: Each card speaks for one living being. Somewhere on the table is that being's partner. Let's find all eight pairs.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and mix them. Lay them face down in four rows.
flow.context: This is the first step of Partner Pairs. Here you lay out the 16 partner cards.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to turn over two cards. 2. Read both aloud. 3. If they are partners, say what each gives the other and keep the pair.
flow.say: Read both cards. Are these two partners? What does each one give the other?
flow.kid: Turn over two cards and read them. Are they partners? Say what each one gives.

ask.q: What would happen to a cow with no microbes in her stomach?
good: She could not digest grass.
She would starve with a full stomach.

flow.parent: If your child matches a pair by memory alone, ask for the reason before they keep it. The reason is the point of the game.
flow.context: This is the main part of Partner Pairs. Here you look for two partners and say what each gives the other.

flow.do: 1. Count the pairs. 2. Lay all eight pairs in a row. 3. Ask which pairs could still live apart, and which could not.
flow.say: Look at the eight pairs. Which partners could still live without each other? Which could not live apart at all?
flow.kid: Count your pairs. Which partners could live apart? Which could not?

check.q: Which pair of partners has become one living being that cannot be separated?
options: A bee and a pumpkin flower
A body cell and the mitochondria inside the cell
A clownfish and a sea anemone
check.why: A bee and a flower meet and part, and a clownfish can swim away from an anemone. A mitochondrion cannot live outside a cell, and the cell cannot live without mitochondria. More than 1.5 billion years ago they were two separate beings.

flow.parent: Not every close pair helps both. A tick on a dog gains while the dog loses. A koel lays her egg in a crow's nest, and the crow raises the koel chick. Natural selection works on all of these.
flow.context: This is the last step of Partner Pairs. Here you ask which partners can still live without each other.

experiments.title: The Bean Generations Test: does one hunter change two groups in the same way?
experiments.question: Two groups of beans start exactly the same, with 15 dark beans and 15 pale beans. One group lives on a dark cloth and one on a pale cloth. The same hunter hunts both for three generations. Do the two groups end up the same?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After three hunts, how many of the 30 beans on the dark cloth will be dark? How many on the pale cloth? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both groups start with 15 dark and 15 pale beans. The same hunter hunts both, and catches exactly 15 beans in every hunt. The beans are scattered over the same area, in the same light. Every survivor gets one young bean of the same colour. Only one thing changes: the colour of the cloth.
results_table: Dark cloth: dark beans, pale beans
Pale cloth: dark beans, pale beans

materials.item: dark beans, such as kala chana or dark rajma
pale beans of about the same size, such as kabuli chana or white lobia
a dark bath towel or bedsheet (brown, maroon, dark blue or black)
a pale bath towel or bedsheet (white or cream)
steel bowls: one for the hunter's catch and two for the spare beans
a notebook, a pencil and a ruler

experiments.safety: Dry beans are a choking risk for children under three. Keep them off the floor afterwards.
experiments.record: Draw a table with four rows, for generations 1, 2, 3 and 4. For each cloth, write the number of dark beans and pale beans at the start of each generation. The two numbers must add up to 30.
experiments.context: In this experiment, dark and pale beans stand for a population of animals, and you are the predator. You hunt them on a dark cloth and on a pale cloth for three generations. Then you count how each group changes.

setup.art: A dark towel spread a little rumpled on a bed, with 15 dark and 15 pale beans scattered across it.
setup.caption: 1. Scatter 15 dark and 15 pale beans on the dark cloth.

setup.art: A child picking up one bean with one hand and dropping the bean into a steel bowl held in the other hand.
setup.caption: 2. The hunter picks up 15 beans, one at a time, as fast as she can.

setup.art: The 15 beans left on the towel sorted into a dark heap and a pale heap, with one new bean being added beside each.
setup.caption: 3. Count the survivors. Give each one a young bean of the same colour.

setup.art: A notebook table with rows for generations 1 to 4 and columns for dark and pale beans.
setup.caption: 4. Write the new numbers. Hunt two more times.

setup.art: The same beans being scattered on a pale towel.
setup.caption: 5. Start again with 15 and 15 on the pale cloth.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the two kinds of beans and the two cloths. 2. Explain the rules of the hunt. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason for each cloth, and write them down.
flow.say: These beans are a population of animals, and you are their predator. You will hunt them for three generations on each cloth. After three hunts, how many of the 30 beans on the dark cloth will be dark? How many on the pale cloth? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the beans and the two cloths. Guess how many dark beans each cloth will have at the end. Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think the two cloths will end the same, or end differently?
good: Pale beans are easy to see on the dark cloth, so I will catch more of them.
I pick without looking at colour, so they will stay half and half.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say the numbers will stay at 15 and 15. Their reason is that the hunter is not trying to choose a colour.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bean Generations Test. You guess how the two groups of beans will end up, before you hunt.

flow.do: 1. Spread the dark cloth on a bed or the floor, about 1 metre wide. Leave it a little rumpled. 2. Count out 15 dark and 15 pale beans. 3. Draw the results table and write 15 and 15 for generation 1. 4. The hunter turns away. Scatter the 30 beans all over the cloth.
flow.say: This is generation 1: fifteen dark and fifteen pale. Turn away while I scatter them. Do not peek.
flow.kid: Spread the dark cloth. Count 15 dark and 15 pale beans. Turn away while a grown-up scatters them.
flow.parent: Folds and a towel's loops give the beans somewhere to hide, as grass does for a real animal. A cloth pulled perfectly flat makes every bean easy to see.
flow.context: In this step of the Bean Generations Test you set up the dark cloth with 30 beans.

flow.do: 1. Say 'go'. The hunter picks up beans one at a time with one hand, and drops each into the bowl. 2. Count aloud and say 'stop' at 15. 3. Collect the 15 survivors from the cloth and sort them by colour. 4. Add one new bean of the same colour for each survivor. 5. Write the new numbers for generation 2.
flow.say: Go! Take the first bean you see each time, as fast as you can. Stop at fifteen. Now let's count who survived. Each survivor has one young of the same colour.
flow.kid: Pick up 15 beans, one at a time, fast. Take the first bean you see. Then count the survivors.

check.q: In the Bean Generations Test, each surviving bean gets one young bean of the same colour. What does this stand for?
options: Young inherit features from their parents
Animals choose their colour
The cloth paints the beans
check.why: Colour is an inherited feature, so a dark parent has dark young. Only the survivors become parents. If you chose 'animals choose their colour', look at the beans: every one kept the colour they started with.

flow.parent: The beans caught are 'eaten' and go back to the spare bowls. Check that the new generation adds up to 30.
flow.context: In this step of the Bean Generations Test you hunt 15 beans on the dark cloth and count the survivors.

flow.do: 1. The hunter turns away. Scatter generation 2. 2. Hunt 15 again, count the survivors, add their young and write generation 3. 3. Do the same once more and write generation 4.
flow.say: Generation 2 is on the cloth. Turn away, then hunt fifteen again. We will do this for generation 3 as well.
flow.kid: Hunt 15 beans again. Count the survivors and add their young. Then hunt once more.
flow.parent: If the numbers stay close to 15 and 15, the beans are too easy to see. Rumple the cloth more, spread the beans wider and ask the hunter to go faster.
flow.context: In this step of the Bean Generations Test you hunt the second and third generations on the dark cloth.

flow.do: 1. Put all the beans back in their bowls. 2. Spread the pale cloth in the same place. 3. Start again with 15 dark and 15 pale beans. 4. Run three hunts exactly as before, and write generations 2, 3 and 4 in the second column.
flow.say: Now the same hunter meets the same starting group in a different place. Fifteen dark and fifteen pale again, on the pale cloth.
flow.kid: Now use the pale cloth. Start with 15 and 15 again. Hunt three times and write the numbers.
flow.parent: Keep everything else the same: the area, the light, the speed and the rule of 15.
flow.context: In this step of the Bean Generations Test you repeat the three hunts on the pale cloth.

flow.do: 1. Draw a line chart. Put generations 1 to 4 along the bottom and the number of dark beans, 0 to 30, up the side. 2. Plot the dark cloth as one line and the pale cloth as another. 3. Label each line.
flow.say: Let's draw both groups on one chart. Each line shows the number of dark beans in one group. Both lines start at fifteen.
flow.kid: Draw a line chart of the dark beans. Draw one line for each cloth. Both start at 15.
flow.parent: A line chart suits these results because each generation follows from the one before.
flow.context: In this step of the Bean Generations Test you draw a line chart of the dark beans on each cloth.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table and the chart together. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 3. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your two lines. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Did any bean change colour during the test?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Did any single bean change colour? Then how did the group change?
good: No bean changed.
The easy-to-see beans were caught, and only the survivors had young.
The group changed because its members were replaced.

ask.q: The hunter was the same on both cloths. Why did the two groups go opposite ways?
good: The place was different.
On each cloth a different colour was hard to see.

flow.parent: In most homes the dark cloth ends with 24 to 30 dark beans. The pale cloth ends with 0 to 6. Write down what you really found. The reason: the hunter catches the beans she sees first, so the beans that match the cloth survive more often. Only survivors have young, and young inherit their parent's colour. So the matching colour becomes more common in each generation. This is natural selection. No bean changed, and the hunter never tried to choose a colour. The model leaves three things out. Real young are never exact copies of a parent. New variations appear through mutation. And real prey also run, hide and learn.
flow.think: What would the two groups look like if they stayed apart for a thousand generations?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Bean Generations Test. You say what your counts show about the two groups of beans.

experiments.title: The Drought Year Test: which beak finds enough food when the seeds change?
experiments.question: A finch with a small beak and a finch with a big beak live on the same island. In a wet year there are many small seeds. In a drought, almost only big seeds are left. Does the same beak find enough food in both years?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which beak will collect enough seeds in the wet year? Which in the drought year? Is one beak better in both? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The same person uses both beaks, with the same hand. Every try lasts 30 seconds. Seeds are lifted one at a time from the plate into a bowl that stands 30 centimetres away. Each beak is tried 3 times on each kind of seed, because one try can be a fluke. Only two things change: the beak and the kind of seed.
results_table: Rice grains in 30 seconds: try 1, try 2, try 3, average
Groundnuts in 30 seconds: try 1, try 2, try 3, average

materials.item: tweezers, for the small beak (a clothes clip also works)
roti tongs (chimta), for the big beak
uncooked rice grains, for the small seeds
groundnuts in their shells, for the big seeds (marbles or whole walnuts also work)
a steel plate and a steel bowl
a phone timer, a ruler, a notebook and a pencil

experiments.record: Draw a table with one row for the tweezers and one row for the tongs. Write the three tries and the average for rice, then for groundnuts. Then write how many seeds each beak collected from the wet year plate and from the drought year plate.
experiments.context: In this experiment, tweezers and roti tongs stand for a small beak and a big beak. You find out which beak collects enough seeds in a wet year and in a drought year.

setup.art: A steel plate of rice grains, a steel bowl 30 centimetres away with a ruler between them, a pair of tweezers and roti tongs.
setup.caption: 1. Put the plate and the bowl 30 centimetres apart.

setup.art: A child lifting one rice grain with tweezers towards the bowl while a phone timer runs.
setup.caption: 2. Lift seeds one at a time for 30 seconds. Count them.

setup.art: The same child lifting a groundnut in the shell with roti tongs.
setup.caption: 3. Try each beak on each seed, 3 times.

setup.art: Two plates side by side: one with many rice grains and 2 groundnuts, one with 20 groundnuts and 3 rice grains.
setup.caption: 4. Make a wet year plate and a drought year plate.

setup.art: A notebook table with a row for tweezers and a row for tongs, filled with counts.
setup.caption: 5. Which beak collects 10 seeds on each plate?

flow.do: 1. Show your child the tweezers, the tongs, the rice and the groundnuts. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: The tweezers are a small beak and the tongs are a big beak. In a wet year there are many small seeds. In a drought, almost only big seeds are left. Which beak will find enough food in each year? Is one beak better in both? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the two beaks and the two seeds. Which beak is better in each year? Say why.
flow.parent: Many children say the big beak is better at everything. Write the guess down and let the test answer it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Drought Year Test. You guess which beak will do well in a wet year and in a drought year.

flow.do: 1. Put 40 rice grains on the plate. Stand the bowl 30 centimetres away. 2. Your child lifts grains one at a time with the tweezers for 30 seconds. Count the grains in the bowl. 3. Do this 3 times, then 3 times with the tongs. 4. Change the rice for 20 groundnuts and try each beak 3 times again. 5. Work out the four averages.
flow.say: One seed at a time, from the plate to the bowl. You have thirty seconds. Ready, go! We will try each beak three times on each seed.
flow.kid: Lift seeds one at a time for 30 seconds. Count them. Try each beak 3 times on each seed.
flow.parent: To find an average, add the three counts and divide by 3. Put the seeds back on the plate after every try. A seed that falls outside the bowl does not count.

check.q: In the Drought Year Test, why do you try each beak 3 times on each seed?
options: One try can be a lucky or unlucky fluke
The beak gets stronger each time
The seeds get lighter each time
check.why: Your hand may slip once or be lucky once. Three tries and an average give a fairer number. If you chose 'the beak gets stronger', remember that the tool is the same each time.

flow.context: In this step of the Drought Year Test you count the seeds each beak can lift in 30 seconds.

flow.do: 1. Make the wet year plate: 60 rice grains and 2 groundnuts, mixed. Give each beak 30 seconds. 2. Make the drought year plate: 3 rice grains and 20 groundnuts, mixed. Give each beak 30 seconds. 3. A bird needs 10 seeds to live. Write 'lives' or 'dies' for each beak in each year.
flow.say: This plate is a wet year. This plate is a drought year. A bird must collect ten seeds in thirty seconds to live. Let's see who lives in each year.
flow.kid: Try each beak on the wet year plate. Then try the drought year plate. Ten seeds means the bird lives.
flow.parent: If both beaks collect 10 on a plate, raise the number a bird needs to 12. Say so in your table. Write what really happens.
flow.context: In this step of the Drought Year Test each beak feeds from two plates: a wet year and a drought year.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 2. Ask what the next generation of beaks would look like after each year. 3. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. If only the survivors have chicks, what beaks will the chicks have after a drought? What about after a wet year?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Is one beak the better beak?
good: No. Each is better in one kind of year.
It depends on which seeds there are.

ask.q: After many drought years in a row, what would most beaks on the island be like?
good: Big, because the big-beaked birds lived and had chicks.
Deep beaks would become common.

flow.parent: In most homes the tweezers lift 12 to 20 rice grains and the tongs only 3 to 6. With groundnuts the result reverses. So the small beak lives in the wet year and the big beak lives in the drought. The reason: a beak is an adaptation to a food, and which beak is fit depends on the food that year. On Daphne Major in 1977, a drought left only large, hard seeds. Finches with deeper beaks could crack them, and survived more often. After heavy rain in 1983, small seeds were plentiful and smaller beaks did better. Our model is not exact. A real big beak cracks hard seeds, while the tongs only grip big ones.
flow.think: An island has drought years and wet years in turn. Why might it be useful for the finch population to keep both kinds of beak?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Drought Year Test. You say what your counts show about the small beak and the big beak.

activities.title: Count the Seeds in One Bhindi: how many young could one plant have?
activities.context: In this activity you count the seeds in one bhindi. Then you work out how many plants could grow from one parent. It leads to the main question of the unit: if so many young are made, which ones survive?

materials.item: one bhindi (lady's finger). A tomato, a capsicum or a lemon also works
a knife and a chopping board, for the grown-up
a steel plate, a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Write your guess, the number of seeds you counted, and your two multiplications.

setup.art: A bhindi cut in half along its length on a chopping board, showing rows of round white seeds.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts the bhindi along its length.

setup.art: A child pushing seeds into groups of five on a steel plate with a fingertip.
setup.caption: 2. Count the seeds in fives.

setup.art: A notebook page with the sum '60 seeds × 20 pods = 1,200 seeds'.
setup.caption: 3. Multiply to find the seeds from one whole plant.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to guess how many seeds are inside the bhindi, and write the guess down. 2. Cut the bhindi in half along its length. 3. Your child pushes the seeds out onto a plate and counts them in fives.
flow.say: How many seeds do you think are inside this one bhindi? Write your guess. Now count them in groups of five.
flow.kid: Guess how many seeds are in one bhindi. Then count them in fives.
flow.parent: Most bhindi hold between 40 and 90 seeds. The seeds in a bhindi from the market are soft and white, because the pod was picked young.
flow.context: This is the first step of Count the Seeds in One Bhindi. Here you guess the number of seeds and then count them.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child that one bhindi plant can give about 20 pods in a season. 2. They multiply their seed count by 20. 3. Then they suppose every seed grows into a plant that also makes that many seeds, and multiply again.
flow.say: One bhindi plant can give about twenty pods. How many seeds is that from one plant? Now suppose every seed grew, and every new plant made as many seeds. How many seeds would there be in the second year?
flow.kid: One plant gives about 20 pods. Multiply your count by 20. Then multiply that answer by itself.
flow.parent: With 60 seeds in a pod: 60 × 20 = 1,200 seeds from one plant. If all grew and did the same, the second year would give 1,200 × 1,200 = 1,440,000 seeds. A calculator is fine for the second sum.
flow.context: In this step of Count the Seeds in One Bhindi you work out how many seeds one plant makes.

flow.do: 1. Ask whether the world is filling up with bhindi plants. 2. Ask what happens to most of the seeds. 3. Write down your child's answer to the last question, to compare with the Bean Generations Test.
flow.say: The world is not covered in bhindi plants. So what happens to most seeds and seedlings? Do you think the ones who live are just lucky, or are some more likely to live? Why?
flow.kid: The world is not full of bhindi. What happens to most seeds? Which ones live, and why?

ask.q: What can stop a seed from becoming a grown plant?
good: Animals eat the seed.
There is no water, light or space.
Disease or insects kill the seedling.

flow.parent: Charles Darwin made the same kind of sum for elephants, the slowest breeders he knew. Every species makes far more young than can survive. Do not give the answer to the last question yet.
flow.context: This is the last step of Count the Seeds in One Bhindi. Here you ask what happens to all the seeds that do not become plants.

activities.title: One New Bean: can a single new variation spread?
activities.context: In the Bean Generations Test, you hunted dark and pale beans on a dark cloth. The dark beans became more common. This activity starts with only one dark bean among 29 pale ones. The single dark bean stands for a new mutation.

materials.item: pale beans, such as kabuli chana
dark beans, such as kala chana
the dark towel or bedsheet from the Bean Generations Test
a steel bowl, a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: For each run, write the number of dark beans at the start of generations 1 to 5.

setup.art: A dark towel scattered with 29 pale beans and a single dark bean, the dark bean circled.
setup.caption: 1. Scatter 29 pale beans and 1 dark bean on the dark cloth.

setup.art: A child hunting beans one at a time into a bowl.
setup.caption: 2. Hunt 15 beans. Each survivor gets one young of the same colour.

setup.art: A notebook showing two rows of numbers: '1, 2, 4, 8, 16' and '1, 0, 0, 0, 0'.
setup.caption: 3. Follow the dark beans for four hunts. Then run the test again.

flow.do: 1. Spread the dark cloth as in the Bean Generations Test. 2. Count 29 pale beans and 1 dark bean. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: This group is all pale, on a dark cloth. One bean has a new mutation and is dark. After four hunts, how many dark beans will there be? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: There are 29 pale beans and 1 dark bean. Guess the number of dark beans after four hunts. Say why.
flow.parent: The rules are the same as in the Bean Generations Test. The hunter turns away, then catches 15 beans, one at a time. Each survivor gets one young of the same colour.
flow.context: This is the first step of One New Bean. Here you guess what will happen to one dark bean among 29 pale beans.

flow.do: 1. Scatter the beans and hunt 15. 2. Count the surviving dark beans and double them. Fill up with pale young until there are 30. 3. Do four hunts and write the number of dark beans each time.
flow.say: Hunt fifteen, as fast as before. Is the dark bean still on the cloth? Then the dark bean has one dark young. Let's follow them for four hunts.
flow.kid: Hunt 15 beans, four times. After each hunt, count the dark beans and double them.
flow.parent: If the dark beans are never caught, they go 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. If the one dark bean is caught in the first hunt, the mutation is lost. The run ends at 0. Both results are real.
flow.context: In this step of One New Bean you hunt four times and follow the number of dark beans.

flow.do: 1. Run the whole test once more from 29 and 1. 2. Compare the two runs. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Let's run it again from the start. Did the same thing happen both times? What decided whether the new variation spread?
flow.kid: Run the test again from the start. Did the same thing happen? Say why or why not.

ask.q: The dark bean appeared before any hunt. Did the hunter cause the mutation?
good: No. The dark bean was there first.
The hunter only decided which beans survived.

ask.q: Can a helpful mutation still be lost?
good: Yes, if the one bean that carries the mutation is caught by bad luck.

check.q: In One New Bean, the single dark bean stands for a mutation. When does a real mutation appear?
options: By chance, when DNA is copied
When the population needs it
When a predator arrives
check.why: A mutation is a chance copying mistake in DNA. It is already there before it turns out to be useful. If you chose 'when the population needs it', remember this. The dark bean was on the cloth before the first hunt.

flow.parent: This shows two things. Selection can spread one new variation through a whole group in a few generations. And chance matters most when a variation is rare.
flow.context: This is the last step of One New Bean. Here you compare two runs and ask what decides whether a mutation spreads.

activities.title: One Wild Plant, Many Vegetables: what did farmers select?
activities.context: In this activity you look at cabbage, cauliflower and knol khol from the kitchen. You find out that farmers made all of them from one wild plant, by choosing which plants became parents.

materials.item: any two of these vegetables: cabbage, cauliflower, knol khol, broccoli. Pictures will do for the ones you do not have
a knife and a chopping board, for the grown-up
a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Draw each vegetable and label the part we eat: leaves, flower buds or stem.

setup.art: A cabbage, a cauliflower and a knol khol side by side on a kitchen counter.
setup.caption: 1. Put the vegetables side by side.

setup.art: A cabbage cut in half showing tightly packed leaves, beside a cauliflower broken into florets.
setup.caption: 2. Find the part we eat: leaves, flower buds or stem.

setup.art: A drawing of a thin wild cabbage plant on a sea cliff with arrows to a cabbage, a cauliflower and a knol khol.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the wild plant in the middle and the vegetables around.

flow.do: 1. Put the vegetables side by side. 2. Cut each in half. 3. Ask which part of the plant we eat in each one. 4. Crush a small piece of leaf or stalk from each and smell it.
flow.say: Which part of the plant do we eat in each of these? Leaves, flower buds or stem? Now smell a crushed piece of each. Do you think these plants are related? Why?
flow.kid: Look at each vegetable. Which part do we eat? Smell a crushed piece of each. Are they related?
flow.parent: A cabbage is a ball of leaves. A cauliflower and a broccoli are masses of flower buds. A knol khol is a swollen stem. All share the same sharp, mustard-like smell.
flow.context: This is the first step of One Wild Plant, Many Vegetables. Here you look at each vegetable and find the part we eat.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child that all these vegetables are one species, bred from a wild cabbage of European sea cliffs. 2. Ask how a farmer could get bigger leaves, using only seeds and patience. 3. Draw the wild plant in the middle of a page, with an arrow to each vegetable.
flow.say: These are all one species. Farmers made them from one wild plant with loose leaves. A farmer wants bigger leaves. She cannot change a plant. What can she do each year with her seeds?
flow.kid: These vegetables are all one species. How could a farmer get bigger leaves, year after year?

ask.q: What does the farmer do each year?
good: She keeps seeds only from the plants with the biggest leaves.
She sows those seeds and chooses again next year.

flow.parent: This is selective breeding. The farmer chooses the parents. Other farmers chose plants with thick stems or big flower heads. Over many hundreds of years, one species gave cabbage, cauliflower, broccoli and knol khol.
flow.context: In this step of One Wild Plant, Many Vegetables you work out how farmers changed one wild plant.

flow.do: 1. Draw two columns: 'Selective breeding' and 'Natural selection'. 2. For each, ask who or what does the selecting, and what gets selected. 3. Ask which is faster, and why.
flow.say: In selective breeding the farmer chooses the parents. In the Bean Generations Test, who or what chose the parents? What is the same in both, and what is different?
flow.kid: Draw two columns. Who chooses the parents in each? What is the same? What is different?

ask.q: What is the same in selective breeding and natural selection?
good: Both need variation.
In both, only some members become parents.
In both, the features are inherited.

flow.parent: Darwin began his book with pigeon breeders for this reason. People changed a species this much in a few hundred years. So the environment can do much more in millions. Indian farmers bred thousands of kinds of rice and hundreds of kinds of mango the same way.
flow.context: This is the last step of One Wild Plant, Many Vegetables. Here you compare selective breeding by farmers with natural selection.

activities.title: One Bird Becomes Two: the Palghat Gap in four drawings
activities.context: In the Bean Generations Test, two groups of beans started the same and ended different. They lived on different cloths. This activity uses that idea to explain how one bird species in the Western Ghats became two.

materials.item: a map of South India, in an atlas or on a phone
a sheet of paper folded into four boxes
pencils or crayons, including blue-grey, white and orange-brown

activities.record: Four drawings in four boxes, each with one sentence underneath.

setup.art: A phone map of South India with a finger pointing at the low gap in the hills between Coimbatore and Palakkad.
setup.caption: 1. Find the Palghat Gap between Coimbatore and Palakkad.

setup.art: A sheet of paper folded into four boxes, the first showing one line of hills with small blue-grey birds all along it.
setup.caption: 2. Fold a page into four boxes. Draw the story step by step.

setup.art: The fourth box showing two hill ranges with a gap, a bird with orange-brown sides on the left and a bird with a white belly on the right.
setup.caption: 3. In the last box, draw the two species of today.

flow.do: 1. Find Coimbatore and Palakkad on the map. 2. Show the Nilgiri hills to the north and the Anamalai hills to the south. 3. Explain that the low land between them is the Palghat Gap, about 30 kilometres wide.
flow.say: The sholakili is a small bird of cold, misty forests on the hilltops. The land in this gap is low and hot. Could a sholakili live in the gap? What would the gap do to a population spread along the hills?
flow.kid: Find the Palghat Gap on the map. A sholakili lives only on cold hilltops. What does the gap do?
flow.parent: The road and the railway from Coimbatore to Palakkad run through this gap. The sholakili stays in cool forests called sholas, high on the hills.
flow.context: This is the first step of One Bird Becomes Two. Here you find the Palghat Gap, which separates two hill ranges in South India.

flow.do: 1. Box 1: draw one line of hills with the same bird all along. 2. Box 2: draw the hot gap splitting the birds into two groups. 3. Box 3: draw a different change in each group, such as belly colour or song. 4. Box 4: draw the two species of today.
flow.say: Draw the story in four boxes. First, one population. Then the gap. Then each group changing in a different way. Last, two species. Write one sentence under each box.
flow.kid: Draw four boxes: one population, the gap, two groups changing, two species. Write a sentence under each.
flow.parent: North of the gap lives the Nilgiri sholakili, with orange-brown sides. South of the gap lives the white-bellied sholakili. Scientists think the two groups have been apart for millions of years. Different mutations appeared on each side, and the two groups could not mix them.
flow.context: In this step of One Bird Becomes Two you draw how one population of birds became two species.

flow.do: 1. Ask how the Bean Generations Test is like this story. 2. Ask how anyone could tell that the two birds are now separate species. 3. Tell your child about the mule.
flow.say: In the Bean Generations Test, what kept the two groups of beans from mixing? What plays that part for the sholakili? How could scientists tell that the two birds are now two species?
flow.kid: What kept the two bean groups apart? What keeps the two birds apart? How do we know they are two species?

check.q: What usually has to happen first, before one species can become two?
options: The population is split into groups that cannot meet
One animal decides to be different
All the food runs out
check.why: While a population can mix, new variations spread through all of it and it stays one species. A barrier stops the mixing, so each group changes in their own way. If you chose 'one animal decides', remember that a species is a whole population, not one member.

flow.parent: Scientists compare the birds' DNA, their songs and their looks. A horse and a donkey show where the line lies. They can have a mule together, but a mule cannot have young. So the two stay separate species.
flow.context: This is the last step of One Bird Becomes Two. Here you compare the two birds with the two groups of beans.

activities.title: The Lemon in the Dupatta: was a mitochondrion once a free bacterium?
activities.context: In this activity you model how a large cell could take in a bacterium, using a lemon and a dupatta. Then you check four clues that Lynn Margulis used to argue that mitochondria were once free bacteria.

materials.item: a lemon, for the bacterium
a dupatta or a thin towel, for the outer skin of the large cell
four slips of paper and a pencil, for the clue cards

activities.record: Draw the lemon inside the pouch of cloth. Label the two layers around it. Write the four clues and tick the ones that fit.

setup.art: Two people holding a dupatta loosely stretched between them, with a lemon resting on top.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the dupatta loosely. Put the lemon on top.

setup.art: A hand pushing the lemon down into the cloth so that the cloth wraps around the lemon.
setup.caption: 2. Push the lemon down. The cloth wraps around the lemon.

setup.art: The cloth twisted closed above the lemon, making a pouch, with labels 'lemon's own skin' and 'cloth layer'.
setup.caption: 3. Twist the cloth closed. Count the layers around the lemon.

setup.art: Four slips of paper with a clue written on each, laid beside the lemon.
setup.caption: 4. Check four clues, one at a time.

flow.do: 1. You and your child hold the dupatta loosely between you. 2. Put the lemon on top. 3. Your child pushes the lemon down into the cloth, then twists the cloth closed above it. 4. Count the layers around the inside of the lemon.
flow.say: The dupatta is the outer skin of a large cell. The lemon is a bacterium, with a skin of their own. Push the bacterium into the cell. How many layers are around the lemon's inside now? Where did each layer come from?
flow.kid: Push the lemon into the dupatta. Twist the cloth shut above the lemon. Count the layers around the lemon.
flow.parent: There are two layers: the lemon's own peel, and a pouch of cloth pinched off from the outside. A real cell takes things in this way. The cell's outer skin, called the membrane, folds in and closes around them.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Lemon in the Dupatta. Here you model a large cell taking in a bacterium.

flow.do: 1. Write one clue on each slip: 'two skins', 'own DNA in a loop', 'makes more by splitting in two', 'DNA matches living bacteria'. 2. For each clue, ask what we should find if Margulis was right. 3. Then read out what scientists found, from the note below.
flow.say: Lynn Margulis said that mitochondria were once free bacteria, taken in by a larger cell. If she was right, what should we find when we look at a mitochondrion? Take the clues one at a time.
flow.kid: Write four clues on four slips. For each, say what we should find if Margulis was right.

ask.q: If mitochondria were once bacteria, how should new mitochondria be made?
good: By one splitting into two, as bacteria do.
The cell should not be able to build one from nothing.

flow.parent: What scientists found. One: a mitochondrion is wrapped in two membranes. Two: a mitochondrion has their own DNA, in a loop like the DNA of bacteria. Three: new mitochondria come only from old ones splitting in two. Four: their DNA matches the DNA of a group of living bacteria. All four clues fit.
flow.context: In this step of the Lemon in the Dupatta you check four clues about where mitochondria came from.

flow.do: 1. Ask what each partner gained. 2. Tell your child about chloroplasts. 3. Ask the last question.
flow.say: The larger cell did not digest the bacterium. What did each partner gain by staying together? Plant cells have a second partner, the green chloroplast. What might a chloroplast once have been?
flow.kid: What did each partner gain? Plant cells also hold green chloroplasts. What were they once?

check.q: Which finding is the strongest evidence that mitochondria were once free bacteria?
options: Their DNA matches the DNA of living bacteria
They are very small
They are found inside cells
check.why: Many things are small and sit inside cells. Only a former bacterium would carry DNA that matches bacteria living today. If you chose 'very small', think of other small parts of a cell that have no DNA of their own.

flow.parent: The bacterium gained food and shelter. The larger cell gained a partner who releases far more energy from food by using oxygen. Chloroplasts were once bacteria that could photosynthesise. Margulis's paper of 1967 was doubted for years, until DNA settled the question.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Lemon in the Dupatta. Here you ask what each partner gained when two cells became one.

projects.title: An Indian Animal at Risk: can they change fast enough?
projects.context: In this three-day project you study one Indian animal whose place is being changed by people. You find their adaptations and work out how long one generation takes. Then you give a three-minute talk on whether natural selection can keep up.

materials.item: a library book or children's encyclopaedia on Indian wildlife, or a phone with a grown-up
a notebook and a pencil
five cards or a chart paper, for the talk

schedule.what: Choose one animal. Find where they live, three adaptations and the problem each solves, and what people are changing in their place.
Find how old the animal is when they first have young, and how many young they have in a year. Compare with a mosquito. Decide whether selection can keep up.
Make five cards and give a three-minute talk. Use one piece of evidence for every point.

projects.record: A notebook page for each day, and five cards for the talk: the animal and their place, their adaptations, what is changing, how fast they breed, and what people could do.

setup.art: A child at a table with an open wildlife book showing a great Indian bustard, writing in a notebook.
setup.caption: 1. Choose an animal and find their adaptations.

setup.art: A notebook page with two rows: 'Mosquito: about 2 weeks' and 'Great Indian bustard: several years, 1 egg a year'.
setup.caption: 2. Compare how fast they breed with a mosquito.

setup.art: A child standing and giving a talk to her family, holding up a card with a drawing of the animal.
setup.caption: 3. Give a three-minute talk with evidence.

flow.do: 1. Help your child choose one animal from the list in the note below. 2. They find where the animal lives, and three adaptations with the problem each solves. 3. They find what people are changing in that place.
flow.say: Choose one animal. Where do they live? Which three features fit them to that place, and which problem does each solve? What are people changing there?
flow.kid: Choose one animal. Find where they live and three adaptations. Find what people are changing there.
flow.parent: Good choices from the south are the Nilgiri tahr of Tamil Nadu and Kerala, and the lion-tailed macaque of the Western Ghats. From the north and west, try the great Indian bustard of Rajasthan and Gujarat, the gharial of the Chambal river or the Ganges river dolphin. From the east, try the olive ridley turtle of the Odisha coast or the red panda of Sikkim. Use the websites of WWF-India, the Bombay Natural History Society or the IUCN Red List.
flow.context: This is day 1 of An Indian Animal at Risk. Here you choose an animal and find their adaptations.

flow.do: 1. Your child finds the age at which the animal first has young. They also find how many young are born in a year. 2. Write these beside a mosquito, who can lay hundreds of eggs and whose young are adults in about two weeks. 3. Ask whether natural selection can keep up with the change.
flow.say: Natural selection needs many young and many generations. A mosquito population met new poisons and adapted in a few years. How long is one generation for your animal? How many young are there to select from?
flow.kid: Find how old your animal is at their first young. Find how many young they have a year. Compare with a mosquito.

ask.q: Why can a slow breeder not adapt quickly to a sudden change?
good: There are few young to select from.
Each generation takes years, and selection needs many generations.
The change comes within one lifetime.

flow.parent: An example: a great Indian bustard female lays only one egg, and not every year, and fewer than 150 birds are left. Many die by flying into power lines. So few chicks are born each year that selection has almost nothing to work on. A species like this needs people to change what they do.
flow.context: This is day 2 of An Indian Animal at Risk. Here you compare how fast your animal breeds with how fast their place is changing.

flow.do: 1. Your child makes five cards: the animal and their place, their adaptations, what is changing, how fast they breed, what people could do. 2. They practise once with a timer. 3. They give the talk to the family, with one piece of evidence on each card.
flow.say: Give your talk in three minutes. For each card, tell us one fact or number that supports what you say.
flow.kid: Make five cards. Practise with a timer. Give your talk in three minutes, with evidence.
flow.parent: A strong talk uses science to support each point. 'Power lines are bad' is weak. 'A bustard sees poorly straight ahead, so she flies into wires' is strong.
flow.context: This is day 3 of An Indian Animal at Risk. Here you give a three-minute talk about your animal.

challenges.title: The Two-Year Beak: build one beak that survives a wet year and a drought
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. In the Drought Year Test, the tweezers collected enough rice in the wet year. The roti tongs collected enough groundnuts in the drought. Here you build one beak that collects enough food in both years.
challenges.problem: Build one tool that lifts at least 10 seeds in 30 seconds from the wet year plate. The same tool must lift at least 10 from the drought year plate.
constraints: Use one hand only. Lift seeds from the plate into a bowl 30 centimetres away, as in the Drought Year Test.
Seeds must be lifted. Sweeping them off the plate does not count.
Build the beak only from home things: ice cream sticks, spoons, clothes clips, rubber bands, card and tape.
Use the same plates as in the Drought Year Test. The wet year plate has 60 rice grains and 2 groundnuts. The drought year plate has 3 rice grains and 20 groundnuts.
materials: ice cream sticks or two old pencils
the rice, groundnuts, plate and bowl from the Drought Year Test
general: Tie two spoons together at the handles with a rubber band, to make wide tongs with a hollow tip.
Tape two ice cream sticks to the arms of a clothes clip, to make a long beak with narrow tips.
Fold a strip of card into a V, to make a springy beak with flat ends.
creative: Make a beak with one narrow tip and one spoon tip, and test which seeds each side can grip.
Make a scoop that lifts many rice grains at once, as a duck's bill strains many small things from water.
Make the tips rough with a strip of tape, sticky side out, and test whether grip matters more than size.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own two-year beak. Draw it, build it and test it on both plates. Did it reach 10 seeds on each? Was it as good as the tweezers at rice, or as good as the tongs at groundnuts?

setup.art: Two steel spoons tied together at the handles with a rubber band, beside a clothes clip with two ice cream sticks taped to its arms.
setup.caption: 1. Build a beak from home things.

setup.art: A child lifting a groundnut with the spoon beak from a plate towards a bowl.
setup.caption: 2. Test the beak on the drought year plate for 30 seconds.

setup.art: The same child trying to lift a rice grain with the same beak from a plate of rice.
setup.caption: 3. Test the same beak on the wet year plate. Then improve it.

flow.do: 1. Set out the two plates as in the Drought Year Test. 2. Remind your child of their results with the tweezers and the tongs. 3. Ask what a beak would need to do well in both years.
flow.say: In the Drought Year Test, each beak did well in only one year. What would one beak need, to lift both rice grains and groundnuts?
flow.kid: Each beak did well in one year only. What would one beak need for both years?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Two-Year Beak challenge. Here you think about what a beak needs to lift both small and big seeds.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws a design. 2. They build it from the home things. 3. They test it for 30 seconds on each plate and write the two counts.
flow.say: Draw your beak first, then build it. Test it on both plates. Write both counts.
flow.kid: Draw your beak. Build it. Test it on both plates and write the counts.
flow.parent: The first design often does well on one plate only. That is useful. Ask which part of the beak caused the problem.
flow.context: In this step of the Two-Year Beak challenge you build your first beak and test it on both plates.

flow.do: 1. Your child changes one thing about the beak. 2. They test again on both plates. 3. They write whether the change helped on each plate.
flow.say: Change one thing only, so we know what made the difference. Then test both plates again.
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test both plates again. Did the change help?
flow.context: In this step of the Two-Year Beak challenge you improve your beak by changing one thing and testing again.

flow.do: 1. Compare the best two-year beak with the tweezers on rice and the tongs on groundnuts. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Your beak works in both years. Is it as good at rice as the tweezers were? Is it as good at groundnuts as the tongs were? What did you give up to get a beak for both?
flow.kid: Is your beak as good as the tweezers at rice? Is it as good as the tongs at groundnuts?

check.q: A beak that can eat many kinds of food is usually a little worse at each one. What is this called?
options: A trade-off
A mutation
A mistake
check.why: A trade-off means gaining one thing by giving up some of another. A crow's all-purpose beak can handle seeds, fruit, insects and scraps, but cracks seeds less well than a parrot's. If you chose 'a mistake', remember that a beak for many foods is very useful when food keeps changing.

flow.parent: Most two-year beaks reach 10 on both plates. But they fall short of the tweezers' rice count and the tongs' groundnut count. A beak for all foods suits a place where food changes often.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Two-Year Beak challenge. Here you compare your beak with the tweezers and the tongs.

items.p: Which of these must be true for natural selection to work?
opts: Members of a population differ from each other
items.why: Selection needs differences to select among. If all were alike, the survivors would be no different from the rest. Choosing 'parents teach' mixes up learning with inherited features.

items.p: An inherited feature that helps a living being survive in their place is called an ____.
items.why: An adaptation solves a problem set by the place, such as heat, cold or a predator.

items.p: Match each adaptation to the problem it solves.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each feature answers one problem of the place. A strong answer can say what would happen without the feature.

items.p: Sort these living beings by the place they are adapted to.
items.a: see items
items.why: The cactus, camel and khejri tree save or find water. The lotus, duck and mangrove live with water all around. The deodar, snow leopard and yak deal with cold and snow.

items.p: True or false: a camel's hump is full of water.
items.why: False. The hump holds fat, which is a food store. Keeping the fat in one place lets the rest of the body lose heat.

items.p: In a hunt on a dark cloth, a group of dark and pale beans became mostly dark. Explain why.
items.a: The hunter saw the pale beans more easily and caught more of them. More dark beans survived. Only survivors had young, and the young had their parent's colour. So each generation had more dark beans.
items.why: A strong answer gives three links: who was caught, who survived, and whose young made the next generation.

items.p: Put the four steps of natural selection in order.
a: Members of a population are born a little different
More young are born than can survive
Those whose features suit the place survive more often
Their features become more common in the next generations
items.why: Variation comes first. Then too many young, then survival of those who fit, then a changed population.
items: Those whose features suit the place survive more often
Members of a population are born a little different
Their features become more common in the next generations
More young are born than can survive

items.p: A tiger's eyes both face forward. What does this help the tiger do?
items.why: Two eyes facing the same way see one thing from two angles, and the brain uses this to judge distance. Choosing 'see behind' describes eyes at the sides, as prey have.

items.p: Three of these are adaptations of prey. Which is the odd one out?
opts: Eyes at the sides of the head
items.why: Side eyes, herds and shells help prey notice or survive an attack. Venom fangs help a predator stop prey.

items.p: Draw a cactus. Label three adaptations that help the cactus live in a dry place.
items.a: A cactus with labels such as: spines in place of leaves, thick stem that stores water, waxy skin, wide shallow roots.
items.why: A strong drawing names each feature and says what it does about water.
items.art: A blank outline of a cactus in sand.

items.p: True or false: in natural selection, each living being changes their own body to suit the place.
items.why: False. Each member keeps the features they were born with. The population changes because some members leave more young than others.

items.p: After a drought, only large, hard seeds are left on an island. Which finches are most likely to survive?
items.why: A deep beak can crack large, hard seeds. Birds with small beaks cannot, and many starve. Choosing 'the youngest' forgets that survival here depends on the beak.

items.p: Two children argue about who survives in nature.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and uses evidence. Examples are a small beak doing better in a wet year, or camouflaged prey surviving. It also says what the other child has right: strength can help in some places.
items.why: The second child is closer to what biologists mean by 'fit'. But strength is one feature that can suit a place, so the first child is not wholly wrong.

views.says: The strongest and biggest animals always survive.
The animals whose features suit their place survive, even if they are small.

items.ask: Which child do you agree with? Give one example as evidence. Then say one thing the other child has right.

items.p: Label a drawing of a lotus plant: floating leaf, stalk with air channels, roots in mud, flower.
a: Roots in mud at the bottom
items.why: The leaf floats in the light. The air channels in the stalk carry air down to the roots in airless mud.
items.art: A lotus plant in a pond drawn large, with blank label lines.

items.p: Name one animal or plant near your home. Describe one adaptation and the problem it solves.
items.a: For example: a house lizard has sticky toe pads. They solve the problem of holding on to smooth walls and ceilings, where the moths are.
items.why: A strong answer names a real feature and a real problem, and links the two.

items.p: Where do brand-new variations come from?
opts: What the living being wishes for
items.why: New variations begin as mutations, which are chance mistakes when DNA is copied. Choosing 'hard practice' is the old idea of Lamarck, which tests have shown to be wrong.

items.p: True or false: a mutation appears because a living being needs one.
items.why: False. Mutations happen by chance. Esther and Joshua Lederberg showed that resistant bacteria were present before the antibiotic was added.

items.p: A farmer sprays the same insect poison every year. After ten years it no longer works. Explain what happened.
items.a: The insects varied. A few could survive the poison because of a chance mutation. They lived and had young, who inherited the mutation. After many generations, most insects in the field could survive the poison.
items.why: A strong answer says the resistant insects were there first, and the poison removed the others. No insect became resistant by being sprayed.

items.p: When a population is split for a very long time, the two groups may become two separate ____.
items.why: Each group changes in their own way. In the end the two can no longer breed together.

items.p: Put these steps in order, to show how one species becomes two.
a: One population lives across a range of hills
A barrier splits the population into two groups
Different mutations and selection change each group
The two groups can no longer breed together
items.why: The split must come before the groups can grow different, because mixing would spread every change to all.
items: Different mutations and selection change each group
The two groups can no longer breed together
One population lives across a range of hills
A barrier splits the population into two groups

items.p: A horse and a donkey can have a mule. A mule cannot have young. What does this tell us?
opts: Horses and donkeys are separate species
Horses and donkeys are one species
A donkey is a young horse
items.why: Members of one species can have young who also have young. A mule cannot, so the two parents belong to separate species. A mule is not a species, because mules cannot breed.

items.p: Sort these features: selected by nature, or selected by people?
items.a: see items
items.why: Farmers and breeders chose the parents for the cauliflower, the mango and the pug. No person chose the parents of the cactus, the tiger or the snow leopard.

items.p: Look at the table. What fraction of the beans on the dark cloth was dark in generation 2?
items.why: In generation 2 there were 20 dark beans out of 30. 20 ÷ 30 = two thirds. Choosing one half is the fraction at the start.

chart.title: Made-up example results: number of dark beans out of 30

items.p: Why is a group whose members are all exactly alike in more danger when their place changes?
items.a: If all are alike, a change that kills one kills all. In a varied group, a few members may have features that suit the new conditions. They survive and the group carries on.
items.why: A strong answer says that variation is what selection works on. With no variation there are no survivors to become parents.

items.p: True or false: farmers made cabbage, cauliflower and knol khol from one wild plant species.
items.why: True. All are one species, bred from a wild cabbage. Farmers saved seed from plants with big leaves, big flower heads or thick stems.

items.p: Draw two islands. Show in three pictures how one bird species could become two.
items.a: Picture 1: birds of one kind on one island, and a few fly to the second. Picture 2: the two groups live apart and each changes. Picture 3: the two groups look different and no longer breed together.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the separation first, then the change, then two species.
items.art: Two blank islands with sea between them.

items.p: Match each word to its meaning.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These five words are needed to explain how species change.
pairs: all of one species living in one place
young born at about the same time
a group that can breed together
people choosing which ones become parents

items.p: Two scientists disagree about what makes a species.
items.a: A strong answer explains each rule and where it works. The breeding rule suits most animals. The DNA rule is needed for bacteria and many plants. It may conclude that no single rule fits all of life.
items.why: This is a real and unsettled argument. Species form slowly, so nature has no sharp line.

views.says: Two groups are separate species if they cannot have fertile young together.
Bacteria never breed in pairs. We must group them by how different their DNA is.

items.ask: Which rule would you use, and for which living beings? Say where the other rule works better.

items.p: A bean model of selection gives each survivor an exact copy as young. What does real life do differently?
opts: Real young differ a little from their parents
Real predators never hunt by sight
items.why: Real young are never exact copies. They get a mix of genes and a few new mutations, so new variation keeps appearing.

items.p: Two species of sholakili live on either side of a wide, hot gap in the hills. Why did the gap matter?
items.a: The sholakili lives only in cool hilltop forest, so the birds could not cross the hot, low gap. The two groups could not breed together. Each side had different mutations and different selection, and over a very long time they became two species.
items.why: A strong answer says the gap stopped the two groups from mixing, which let their differences add up.

items.p: Lynn Margulis said mitochondria were once free bacteria. Give two pieces of evidence that support her.
items.a: Any two: mitochondria have their own DNA in a loop, like bacteria. New ones are made only by old ones splitting in two. They have two membranes. Their DNA matches that of living bacteria.
items.why: A strong answer gives findings, and says why each is what we would expect of a former bacterium.

items.p: A mitochondrion is wrapped in two membranes. How did Lynn Margulis's idea explain the outer one?
opts: From the larger cell's own membrane
It grew to keep out cold
It is a shell left from an egg
It was added by a virus
items.why: When a cell takes something in, the cell's own membrane folds around it and pinches off. So the bacterium kept their own membrane and gained a second one.

items.p: Two biologists disagree about how much cooperation matters in evolution.
items.a: A strong answer gives each side's evidence. Mutation and selection are measured in finches and bacteria. Joining made the first complex cell, plant cells, lichens and corals. It may say both happen, and ask how often each does.
items.why: Both kinds of evidence are real. Most biologists think joining is rare but changed life greatly when it happened.

views.who: A biologist who follows Darwin closely
views.says: Nearly all change comes from small mutations and competition for food and mates.

views.who: A biologist who follows Lynn Margulis
views.says: The biggest steps came when different living beings joined into one, as in the first complex cell.

items.ask: Which biologist do you find more convincing? What evidence does each have? Could both be right?

items.p: True or false: you inherit your mitochondria from your mother.
items.why: True. The egg cell is full of mitochondria, and those in the sperm are not passed on. So mitochondria come down the mother's line.

items.p: Design a fair test with beans and a cloth: does a group change faster when the hunter catches more?
items.a: Run the hunt twice from 15 dark and 15 pale on the same cloth. In one run catch 10 of 30 each time, in the other catch 20 of 30. Keep the hunter, the cloth, the light and the number of hunts the same. Compare the number of dark beans after three hunts.
items.why: A strong design changes only the number caught, keeps the rest the same, and says what will be counted. Survivors must have enough young to bring the group back to 30.

items.p: Mosquitoes adapt to a new poison in a few years. Elephants could not. What is the main reason?
opts: Mosquitoes have a new generation every few weeks
Poison is weaker on small animals
items.why: Selection works generation by generation. A mosquito generation takes weeks and an elephant generation takes about 20 years. Elephants do vary, so 'do not vary' is wrong.

items.p: Sort these pairs: do both partners gain, or does one gain while the other is harmed?
items.a: see items
items.why: The bee, the coral and the fig each give and get. A tick takes blood and gives nothing. A koel leaves her egg for a crow to raise, and the crow's own chicks may lose out.
items: koel and the crow who raises her chick

items.p: Hunters killed elephants with tusks for 15 years. Afterwards, more females were born without tusks. Explain why.
items.a: Some females had no tusks because of an inherited variation. Hunters killed elephants with tusks, so tuskless females survived more often. They had calves, and their daughters often inherited no tusks. So the share of tuskless females went up.
items.why: A strong answer says the tuskless variation was already there, and the hunting changed who survived to have calves. No elephant lost her tusks to escape hunters.

items.p: A helpful mutation appears in one animal. Is the mutation certain to spread through the population?
opts: No, bad luck may kill that animal
Only if the animal wants that
items.why: While a variation is rare, chance matters a great deal. The one animal who carries the mutation may be eaten before having young, as the single dark bean sometimes is.

items.p: True or false: bacteria alive today are less evolved than humans.
items.why: False. Every species alive today has an equally long history. Bacteria have been adapting for more than 3.5 billion years, and live in more places than any animal.

items.p: Draw a large cell taking in a small bacterium. Show the two membranes around the bacterium afterwards.
items.a: Three steps. The large cell's membrane folds in around the bacterium. The fold pinches off. The bacterium now sits inside with their own membrane, plus a second one from the large cell.
items.why: A strong drawing shows where the second membrane came from: the outer skin of the larger cell.
items.art: A large blank cell outline with a small oval beside it.

items.p: When two species change over generations in answer to each other, scientists call it ____.
items.why: Deer and tigers, figs and fig wasps, and flowers and bees have each shaped the other.

items.p: In three of these pairs, both partners gain. Which pair is the odd one out?
opts: Fungus and alga in a lichen
items.why: A mosquito takes blood and may pass on disease, so the human loses. In the other three pairs, each partner gives the other something useful.

items.p: A weed in rice fields looks almost exactly like young rice. Farmers weed by hand. Why did this look spread?
opts: Farmers pulled out the weeds that looked different
items.why: Weeds that looked unlike rice were seen and pulled out. Weeds that happened to look like rice survived and set seed. The farmers' hands did the selecting, without meaning to.

items.p: Some fish that live in dark wells have no eyes. Is losing eyes a step backwards? Give your reasons.
items.a: No. In total darkness eyes are useless, and they cost energy to build. Fish without eyes had more energy for other things and left more young. The fish became better fitted to the dark.
items.why: A strong answer says that 'fit' depends on the place, and that evolution has no forwards or backwards.

quiz.p: Which list gives the things natural selection needs?
opts: Variation, inheritance and more young than can survive
quiz.why: Selection needs differences that are inherited, and more young than the place can support. Choosing 'wanting, trying and learning' is the old idea that effort changes what is inherited.

quiz.p: A beetle population goes from mostly green to mostly brown in 20 generations. What changed?
opts: The share of brown beetles in the population
Each green beetle slowly turned brown
The beetles chose a new colour
quiz.why: More brown beetles survived and had young in each generation, so their share grew. No single beetle changed colour.

quiz.p: Why does a cactus have spines where most plants have flat leaves?
opts: Spines lose far less water than flat leaves
quiz.why: Water escapes from a leaf's surface, and a spine has very little surface. The green stem makes the food. Spines also keep thirsty animals away.

quiz.p: A plant has large floating leaves and stalks full of air channels. Where does this plant most likely live?
quiz.why: Floating leaves reach the light on water, and air channels carry air to roots in airless mud. Both are adaptations to a wet place.

quiz.p: A chital deer has eyes at the sides of the head. What is the main gain?
opts: Seeing danger from almost all around
Judging the distance for a leap onto prey
quiz.why: Side eyes give prey a very wide view. Forward eyes, which judge distance, are found in predators such as tigers and owls.

quiz.p: Over many generations, deer become faster. What is likely to happen to the tigers who hunt them?
opts: Faster or stealthier tigers leave more young
Tigers stay the same for ever
Each tiger trains her legs for her cubs
quiz.why: Only the tigers who can still catch deer eat well and raise cubs. So the prey select the predator, as the predator selects the prey. This is coevolution.

quiz.p: When does a helpful mutation first appear?
opts: As soon as the place changes
quiz.why: A mutation is a chance copying mistake. It is already present when conditions change, and selection then spreads it.

quiz.p: What usually has to happen first for one species to split into two?
opts: Two groups are kept apart for long
quiz.why: While groups can mix, they stay one species. A barrier lets each group change in their own way until they can no longer breed together.

quiz.p: Which fact supports the idea that mitochondria were once free bacteria?
opts: They have their own bacteria-like DNA
They are found only in plants
They are the biggest part of a cell
quiz.why: Mitochondria carry a loop of DNA that matches living bacteria, and they multiply by splitting. They are found in animals, plants and fungi.

quiz.p: After one year of drought, the finches on an island had deeper beaks on average. Why?
opts: More deep-beaked birds survived and had chicks
Each finch stretched their beak on hard seeds
quiz.why: Birds with shallow beaks could not crack the hard seeds, and many starved. The survivors passed deeper beaks to their chicks. No bird's own beak grew.

quiz.p: In biology, what does 'fittest' mean in the phrase 'survival of the fittest'?
quiz.why: Fit means fitting the place. A small beak is fittest in a wet year and a deep beak in a drought. Strength is only sometimes what suits a place.

quiz.p: Why can mosquitoes adapt to a poison faster than bustards adapt to power lines?
opts: Mosquitoes have many young, a few weeks apart
Power lines are stronger than poison
quiz.why: Selection needs many young to select among, over many generations. A mosquito lays hundreds of eggs and a generation takes weeks. A bustard lays one egg a year.

applications: Doctors ask you to finish a full course of antibiotics, and not to take them for colds. Every use of an antibiotic selects for bacteria that can survive that antibiotic.
A new flu vaccine is made every year, because flu viruses mutate. The ones our bodies do not recognise spread.
Farmers are advised to change the insect poison they use from season to season. Then no one poison selects resistant insects for long.
Plant breeders in India used selective breeding to make rice that survives flooding, such as Swarna-Sub1. They also made rice that copes with drought, such as Sahbhagi Dhan.
Seed banks, such as the National Gene Bank in New Delhi, store many thousands of crop varieties. They keep the variation that future breeding and selection will need.
Wildlife corridors join separated forests, so that elephants and tigers from different groups can meet and mix their genes.
Engineers copy natural selection in computers. A program makes many varied designs, keeps the best and varies them again. NASA flew a spacecraft antenna designed this way in 2006.
