open_questions.q: Can a new species form without any barrier, in the middle of the parent population?
open_questions.why_open: A few cases in fish and insects suggest that this can happen. Scientists disagree about how often this happens.

open_questions.q: Which large cell took in the bacterium that became the mitochondrion, and how?
open_questions.why_open: DNA points to a group of microbes called Asgard archaea, first found in 2015. One was grown in a laboratory in 2020, after twelve years of work. How the joining happened is still argued over.

open_questions.q: If life on Earth began again, would evolution give similar animals and plants?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists think chance events would send life a different way each time. Others point out that eyes and wings evolved many times over. Nobody can rerun the whole experiment.

open_questions.q: How much of the difference between species is due to selection, and how much to chance?
open_questions.why_open: Most changes in DNA seem to make no difference to survival. Scientists are still measuring what share of evolution selection explains.

open_questions.q: How often does a new habit come first, with the genes changing afterwards?
open_questions.why_open: There are good examples, such as milk drinking in humans. Scientists disagree about whether this is common or rare.

jokes.j: What did the finch say when the small seeds ran out?

jokes.j: Why did the mitochondrion never pay rent?

maths.problem: In Count the Seeds in One Bhindi, one pod held 60 seeds, and one plant gives about 20 pods. How many seeds does one plant make? If every seed grew and did the same, how many seeds would there be the next year?
maths.answer: 1,200 seeds from one plant, and 1,440,000 seeds the next year.
maths.explain: 60 × 20 = 1,200 seeds from one plant. Suppose all 1,200 grew into plants that each made 1,200 seeds. There would be 1,200 × 1,200 = 1,440,000 seeds.
maths.context: This is about Count the Seeds in One Bhindi. There you count the seeds in one pod and work out how many young one plant could have.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying shows how fast a population would grow if every young one lived. The huge answer tells us that most young do not survive.

maths.problem: On the dark cloth, the group always has 30 beans. It had 15 dark beans in generation 1 and 20 in generation 2. What fraction of the group was dark each time?
maths.answer: One half in generation 1, and two thirds in generation 2.
maths.explain: 15 out of 30 is 15 ÷ 30 = one half. 20 out of 30 is 20 ÷ 30 = two thirds. So the dark share grew from one half to two thirds in one hunt.
maths.context: This is about the Bean Generations Test. There you hunt 15 dark and 15 pale beans on a dark cloth and a pale cloth, for three generations. These are made-up results.

chart.title: Made-up example results: number of dark beans out of 30

maths.why_maths: A fraction shows how common a feature is in the whole group. That is what natural selection changes.

maths.problem: On the pale cloth, generation 2 had 22 pale beans out of 30. What percentage of the group was pale? Round to the nearest whole number.
maths.explain: 22 ÷ 30 = 0.733. Multiply by 100 to get 73.3. So about 73 per cent of the group was pale.
maths.context: This is about the Bean Generations Test. There you hunt 15 dark and 15 pale beans on a dark cloth and a pale cloth, for three generations. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Percentages let you compare groups fairly, even when the groups are of different sizes.

maths.problem: On the dark cloth, the number of dark beans went 15, 20, 26, 28. The rise was 5, then 6, then only 2. Why did the rise slow down, when the hunter did not change?
maths.answer: By generation 3 only 4 pale beans were left. So the hunter had to catch mostly dark beans to reach 15.
maths.explain: In generation 3 there were 26 dark and 4 pale beans. Even if the hunter caught all 4 pale beans, 11 of the 15 caught had to be dark. With few pale beans left to remove, the dark share could not rise much more.
maths.context: This is about the Bean Generations Test. There you hunt 15 dark and 15 pale beans on a dark cloth and a pale cloth, for three generations. These are made-up results.

chart.title: Made-up example results: number of dark beans out of 30

maths.why_maths: Reading how a line bends tells you more than its end point. Here it shows that selection slows down as the variation runs out.

maths.problem: In One New Bean, the dark beans doubled after every hunt: 1, 2, 4, 8. If they keep doubling, after how many hunts would the dark beans pass the group size of 30?
maths.explain: Keep doubling: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. The fifth doubling gives 32, which is more than 30. So one new variation could fill a group of 30 within 5 generations.
maths.context: This is about One New Bean. There a single dark bean among 29 pale beans stands for a new mutation. You follow the dark beans for four hunts.
maths.why_maths: A doubling pattern shows how quickly one rare mutation can spread once selection favours it.

maths.problem: In the 1977 drought on Daphne Major, fewer than 1 in 5 of about 1,200 medium ground finches survived. Take 180 as a round example. What fraction survived, and what percentage died?
maths.answer: 3 in every 20 survived, which is 15 per cent. So 85 per cent died.
maths.explain: 180 ÷ 1,200 = 18 ÷ 120 = 3 ÷ 20. As a percentage, 3 ÷ 20 = 15 per cent. 100 − 15 = 85, so 85 per cent died.
maths.context: This is about the real drought behind the Drought Year Test. In that test you find out which beak collects enough seeds when the food changes.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that natural selection can be watched as it happens? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: In 1859 Charles Darwin wrote that natural selection works too slowly for anyone to watch. For more than a hundred years, most scientists agreed. In 1973 Rosemary and Peter Grant began work on Daphne Major, a tiny island in the Galápagos. They caught the finches, put coloured rings on their legs and measured every beak. In 1977 almost no rain fell. The small, soft seeds ran out, and only large, hard seeds were left. Of about 1,200 medium ground finches, fewer than one in five lived. The Grants and their student Peter Boag compared the survivors with the birds who had died. The survivors' beaks were a little deeper on average, less than a millimetre, but deep enough to crack the hard seeds. Their chicks inherited deeper beaks. After heavy rains in 1983, small seeds were plentiful, and birds with smaller beaks did better. The Grants kept measuring for 40 years. Natural selection had been seen and measured, one season at a time.
how_we_found_out.who: Rosemary Grant and Peter Grant, biologists born in Britain, with their student Peter Boag
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That natural selection is always too slow to see in one human lifetime. The Grants measured a change in the average beak after a single dry year.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman and a man sitting on bare volcanic rock, the woman holding a small brown finch gently while measuring the beak with callipers, a notebook open beside them.

roots.context: We have learned how natural selection fits living beings to their places, how species split, and how partners join. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Bean Generations Test, no bean changed colour. Yet after three hunts, one group was mostly dark and the other mostly pale. Each hunt removed the beans that were easy to see, and only survivors left young. So a group of living beings can change over generations while no member changes.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'the camel adapted to the desert', as if each camel reshaped their own body to suit the sand. That way of speaking hides where the change happens. A camel does not change in her own lifetime. The change happens from one generation to the next, depending on which members of the group go on to have young.
deep_truth.evidence: On the dark cloth, the count of dark beans rose from 15 to about 28 in three hunts. On the pale cloth the count fell towards 0. Every bean kept the colour they began with. On Daphne Major, the average finch beak grew deeper after the 1977 drought, because shallow-beaked birds died. Each living bird kept the beak they had.

three.who_am_i: Every one of your ancestors lived long enough to have a child, all the way back to the first cells. Inside your cells live mitochondria, whose ancestors were free bacteria.
three.what_is_life: Life makes more young than can survive, and makes each one a little different. Those differences are how life comes to fit new places.
three.what_is_this_world: Each place shapes the living beings in it, and they also shape the place and each other. Over many generations, tigers caught the slower deer, so deer became faster. In the same way, deer escaped the noisier tigers, so tigers became better at creeping up quietly.

roots.thread: All living beings descend from one ancestor. Chance mutations make each family line a little different, and different places keep different variations. In this way one species becomes two, and two become many. Sometimes two different kinds of living being join together instead. A bacterium and a larger cell did this long ago, and together they became the first complex cell. So life has both branched apart into new species and joined together into new kinds of cell.

teachings.source: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1859), final paragraph
teachings.teaching: Darwin describes a tangled bank full of plants, birds, insects and worms, all depending on each other. His last words are: 'from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved.'
teachings.link: This is the unit's science in its first author's words: one beginning, many forms, and the change still going on.

teachings.source: Udana 1.1, a discourse of the Buddha on dependent arising
teachings.teaching: When this is, that is. From the arising of this comes the arising of that.
teachings.link: No species has their shape by themselves. A cactus has spines because of the dry places where cacti lived. A chital has an alarm call because tigers hunt chital. Each feature depends on the place and on the other beings in it.

teachings.source: Peter Kropotkin, Mutual Aid: A Factor of Evolution (1902)
teachings.teaching: Kropotkin watched animals through Siberian winters. He wrote that in harsh places, the animals who help each other are the ones who survive best.
teachings.link: Lynn Margulis later showed that helping can go as far as two beings becoming one cell. Cooperation is one of the things natural selection keeps.

science.text: All living beings on Earth share one ancestor.
Mitochondria descend from bacteria that joined a larger cell more than 1.5 billion years ago.
The choices and behaviour of living beings often change first. Genes that suit the new way of life become common afterwards.

other_view.who: Jacques Monod, a French biologist, in Chance and Necessity (1970)
other_view.view: Monod wrote that every new feature of life begins as a chance mistake in DNA, kept or removed by selection. He saw no plan, no purpose and no oneness behind it. In his view humans appeared by chance in a universe that has no interest in them.

practice.title: The unbroken line
practice.say: Let's sit still and look at one hand. Your hand was built from instructions you got from your parents. They got theirs from their parents. Breathe in slowly, and think of one generation back. Breathe out. With each breath, go back one more generation. Every one of them lived long enough to have a child. Not one link is missing, all the way back to the first cells. Now look out of the window at any bird or plant. Their line is unbroken too, and far back it joins yours.
practice.kid: Sit still and look at your hand. Breathe in slowly and think of your mother. Breathe out. With each breath, think one generation further back. Every one of them lived to have a child. Now look at a bird or a plant. Their line is unbroken too.

ask: No bean changed, yet the group changed. Where exactly did the change happen?
Your line of ancestors and a crow's line meet somewhere far back. What does that make you and the crow?
Your cells hold partners that were once free bacteria. Where do 'you' end and 'they' begin?
If tigers shaped the deer and deer shaped the tigers, can either be understood alone?

playtest: The experiments, activities and games were reasoned through step by step for a city flat. They have not yet been tried at home. The Bean Generations Test (core) needs 30 dark and 30 pale beans of about the same size. It also needs a dark and a pale towel or bedsheet. The test works only if the cloth is a little rumpled and the hunter is quick. On a flat cloth every bean is easy to see, and the numbers stay near 15 and 15. The step says what to do then. Expect the dark cloth to end with 24 to 30 dark beans. The Drought Year Test (core) needs tweezers or a clothes clip, roti tongs, rice and 20 groundnuts in shells. Counts differ a lot between children. So the step says to raise the number a bird needs if both beaks pass. One New Bean can end at 0 dark beans if the single dark bean is caught. That is a real result. Count the Seeds in One Bhindi and One Wild Plant, Many Vegetables need a grown-up with a knife. The numbers in the made-up results agree across the experiment, the maths and the worksheets. Real-world facts (finch, elephant, Kolli Hills, bustard, museum and citation details) were checked on 17 Nov 2026. The finch survivor count and beak figure were softened, and the finch arrival date and the lactase date were made less exact. The films were handled separately; find and watch them first.
